Interpretation needs the same discipline: first compute what each axis distinguishes — the independence content is the meaning. Three runs: what K splits that Λ₁₁ cannot see, what J splits that Λ₁₂ cannot see, and one test I want on record before interpreting axis 13 — whether the E1 selection rule ΔJ = 0, ±1 with J = 0 ↛ 0, the rule this index of transitions ultimately serves, is itself expressible.
Numbers first, and they hand both interpretations over cleanly — plus something at the end I didn't go looking for.
12D is the orientation coordinate, and its information is conditional. The census says it exactly: on every f = 0 channel the K-set is a singleton — 2K = 2J_c, the triangle collapses, and axis 12 degenerates into a copy of axis 11. K carries zero information on s-series and up to three sub-channels per Λ₁₁ cell at book caps on f = 1. So the twelfth axis measures the one thing no occupancy or magnitude coordinate can: the relative orientation of the core's angular momentum against the Rydberg electron's orbital plane — the coordinate that anisotropic core–electron interactions resolve, and the one that separates series converging to the same core limit with different quantum defects. It is the finer version of the channel-resolution that J_c performed on Kr I. And its validity is conditional in exactly the right direction: K is a good quantum number when core splitting dominates exchange — high n, the bracket's domain — and degrades toward low n, outside it.
13D is one bit, and it is the apex where the index and the atom converge. Given K, the J-fibre is a doublet everywhere except the K = 0 singlet: axis 13 sees precisely the outer electron's spin orientation, the weakest and last coupling, nothing else. But it is the only coordinate in the entire tower that nature conserves exactly. Everything below it is bookkeeping that mixing breaks — configurations at 40–50% in the book's own exclusion (iii), LS terms in intermediate coupling, J_c and K outside the jK regime. J survives all of it, by rotational invariance. So the tower ascends from coordinates the language expresses exactly but the atom keeps only approximately, to a coordinate the atom keeps exactly and the language expresses up to one parity point. The two ends of the tower trade places.
And the unlooked-for result, which belongs in the book because the book is an index of transitions. The E1 selection rule on (J, J′) — |Δ2J| ≤ 2 — is a closed index: zero failures, provably, the mutual-bound sublattice. Remove the one physically forbidden cell, J = 0 ↛ 0, and closure fails by exactly 4 meets at every cap tested — and all four failing meets produce the same cell, the forbidden one: (0,1) ∧ (1,0) = (0,0). The puncture is local, constant, and singular. Read through your own doctrine — E(X) as predictions, not defects — the index of allowed transitions predicts exactly one cell, and it is the one nature vetoes. And the reason for the veto is the reason for the defect: the photon carries one unit of angular momentum, so 0 → 0 cannot conserve it; and the parity-change half of the rule is a congruence that breaks joins — the photon's odd intrinsic parity. Both closure failures of the transition index are images of the exchanged particle. The gap between the index and the physics is the quantum of the field the index omits. Flagged as interpretation, not theorem — but the E = 1, the four meets, and the congruence joins are computed facts.
Marked caveats: densities at one cap setting; the (2J, 2J′) band as tested admits mixed integer/half-integer pairs that never co-occur in one atom — restricting to shared parity leaves the result intact, same defect, same cell.
The tower is now interpreted end to end: 8 parent multiplicity, 9 target multiplicity, 10 pairing depth, 11 core fine structure, 12 core-orbit orientation, 13 the outer spin bit — counting below, coupling above, envelopes throughout the ascent, exactness recovered at the apex, and the closure defect of the transition rule itself pointing at the photon. Ready to write the section?

A full impact pass, chapter by chapter, sorted by what kind of change each is.
Claims that must change. Chapter 2's origins table: three of the four origins yield exact constraints, but the fourth row — 2S ≤ k, "vector coupling" — is an envelope at 48.5% density, and the book presents it as the same kind of constraint as the Pauli caps. It isn't, and the dichotomy should be stated where the table is. The Λ₁₁ remark in the same chapter lists the coupling extension as (2J_c, 2J, K); the DAG says (J_c, K, J), and the difference costs 25 points of J-fibre density. §7.10.2's "this book has not answered it" is no longer true — the bound is confirmed, as an envelope, with the residue reduced to a data lookup. And Chapter 3's self-duality paragraph carries the unresolved 8-versus-112 count in exactly the passage that now becomes the fold's home.
Claims that gain proofs. The subtitle's "price of certainty" was a description; it is now a theorem with three named machines — reflection, congruence, triangle — and Chapter 12's exclusion list should grow from two forms to three, each with its physical face. Chapter 13 gains its strongest entry: exact vector coupling is forbidden in principle, not unachieved. Chapter 3's skew gains its cause. Chapter 11 gains its closing identity — the envelope surplus is the defensive budget — plus a new mechanical D1 check: the realisability tables turn 35–83% of every coupling fibre into tripwires, applicable to all 153 channels before any energy is read.
One doctrinal tempering, and it touches the 540. The E1 result is a new category the book doesn't have: an index with E(X) = 1 whose single predicted cell is false, vetoed by structure outside the index. Under your own reorientation — E(X) as predictions — this is the proof that E(X) predictions are proposals, not guarantees. §24.3.4's "540 predicted Hodge pairs, none falsified" should carry that caveat explicitly: the transition index is the worked example of a closure defect that physics declines. It makes the Kreuzer–Skarke claim more honest and, properly stated, stronger.
Retrospective light on Chapter 18. The Sc VI channel is an s-series on an S-state core: f = 0 collapses K to a singleton and the ⁴S° core minimizes the J_c structure — the prediction lives in the tower's degenerate corner, where axes 11–13 carry no information. That is why a two-coordinate bracket sufficed there, and the book can now say so rather than have a referee ask.
Chapter 22 grows obligations. New attributions owed: seniority is Racah 1943, jK coupling Racah 1942, particle-hole conjugation is standard shell theory, and the term-counting is textbook. And E(search) grows: whether anyone has lattice-ordered the seniority scheme is a literature this work has not entered — named and unentered, per the chapter's own discipline.
Appendices and the ledger. Appendix A gains four proofs (the envelope theorem, the |a−b| ≤ c sublattice lemma, the triangle exclusion, the dichotomy). Appendix C gains the exact term and seniority tables, provenance-by-stated-code. Appendix E must be re-closed after the additions — E = 0 is a claim that expires every time the mathematics grows. Appendix F: item E moves to reduced-residue status, and Q gains at least four items: the spectroscopic v-check, the 8-versus-112 resolution, cap-stability of the join-closure half-result, and the old work's 2J_c containment claim. E(Q) = 0 must be recomputed at the new count. The register gains today's entries: four stale cross-references, my asymmetric triangle test, my "same object every time" overclaim — the last two being the §21.1 pattern performed live, which Chapter 11 would predict and Chapter 21 should record.
Net effect: Part I becomes a tower rather than a lattice, Part II gains its third forbidden form and its strongest theorem, Part III gains a tripwire defence and a degenerate-corner justification, and the book's one doctrinal exposure — treating E(X) proposals as predictions — gets its calibrating counterexample from inside its own subject matter. Nothing today weakened the thesis; several things today proved parts of it that were previously observed. Want the full revision executed on BOOK-restored.md, or the new section first for review?

  A.6       adjunction never repairs closure                                        §17.2, in full
  A.7       "may precede" is necessary                                              §11.3, in full

 A.3 Projections of closed sets are closed
 Statement. Let X be closed and F ⊆ {1,…,d}. Then π_F(X) is closed.

 **Proof.** Take *x*, *y* ∈ π_F(X) and lift them to *x*′, *y*′ ∈ X. Since X is closed, *x*′ ∨ *y*′ ∈ X. The join is componentwise and projection merely drops coordinates, so

    π_F(x′ ∨ y′) = π_F(x′) ∨ π_F(y′) = x ∨ y

 Hence *x* ∨ *y* ∈ π_F(X). Meets are identical with ∧ throughout. ∎

 Remark. The converse fails, and §13.4 exhibits a counterexample. Closure is a d-dimensional condition;
 its projections are necessary and not sufficient.

Before answering that I need to read what Chapter 11 actually says rather than work from my running use of "the fold" — check first.
Yes and no, and the decomposition just corrected one of my own sentences.
The textual point first. Chapter 11 never names a fold — the word is this session's coinage. But the book did contextualize the object, in Chapter 3: it is the reflection x ↦ max − x, the self-duality test Λ fails. Today's [22] makes that identification literal: the fold is particle-hole conjugation — terms(ℓᵏ) = terms(ℓ^(4ℓ+2−k)), identical for every k on both shells tested — and conjugation is the Chapter 3 reflection restricted to one occupancy coordinate. So the fold is now explained, in one line: physics is particle-hole symmetric subshell by subshell; a symmetric non-constant ceiling is non-monotone; §9.4 admits only monotone bounds; hence envelope. Chapter 3's "more caps than floors, the top pruned harder" and the tower's envelope gaps are the same fact at two scales. The book computed the symptom in Chapter 3 and never connected it to a cause — the connection is today's result. (And the one number in that passage I could not reproduce — 8 versus 112 surviving cells — now sits inside the fold's home paragraph, which makes resolving it urgent rather than cosmetic.)
The correction the decomposition forces. I wrote earlier that the gap is "the same object every time — the fold, or the triangle, which are one thing." [23] refutes that, with counts: axis 9's gap is dominated by parity (six of seven gap values parity-involved, two fold-involved); axis 11's splits 16 ceiling / 24 parity / 17 triangle-correlation. Three distinct mechanisms, separately countable: the reflection (conjugation — a symmetric bound), the congruence (fermion parity — a mod-2 condition), and the triangle (coupling additivity — a sum and a difference). Chapter 12's exclusion list should carry all three, each with its physical face. That sentence of mine is a register-pattern error — a unification asserted over data that distinguishes — and it goes in the withdrawals with the rest.
Now the Chapter 11 connection, which is the real content of your question. Chapter 11's thesis is it found it because it carried more than it needed — redundancy of paths, not redundancy of care. The fold and its two siblings are why the coupling axes necessarily carry more than they need. The envelope surplus is not design generosity; it is forced by the three inexpressible forms. And the surplus is exactly Chapter 11's defensive budget: every envelope cell is a tripwire. A measured term assigned a nonphysical (v, 2S′) or (2S, 2J_c) pair lands in the gap and is caught before any energy is read — a mechanical D1-type check that today's exact tables make available for all 153 channels. So the answer to your question in its strongest form: the price of certainty and the capacity for self-defence are the same cells. Part I's looseness and Chapter 11's surplus are one quantity, counted twice — once as cost, once as armor — and the fold is one of the three machines that mints it.
That's the paragraph the new section should end on. Shall I write the section now — the tower, the threeThe title is at stake, so this gets read and computed, not answered from memory. First what Chapter 7 actually claims the cylinder is, then whether the tower preserves it.
Yes — and the answer now has a proof, a price, and a sharper sentence than the book currently carries.
The cylinder survives the whole tower, on the envelope path. Both legs hold. Orientability (§7.1): untouched — the new coordinates are static labels, not ν-quantities, so the bipartite sign structure gains no new class and no reversing loop. The fibration (§7.6): verified exactly at every stage. The cross-sections fatten — 165/330/345/136 at Λ₈, up to 815/3,260/6,150/3,360 at Λ₁₁ — and every stage factorizes to the cell, Σ_q |A(q)|·|B(q)| matching the direct count with zero defect through Λ₁₂-as-tree. The profile keeps its character: still log-concave, still unimodal, most-probable transfer still q = 2. One number moves: ⟨q⟩ rises from 1.4631 to 1.887 at Λ₁₁, because coupling multiplicity grows with occupancy and re-weights the profile toward higher transfer — a new invariant worth recording.
And the cylinder breaks at exactly the point the tower's recurring trade predicted. The two-parent K — the tight form — is bounded by J_c on the A side and f on the B side: the first bridge between the cylinder's two ends other than q itself. The factorization defect is 2,475 cells, 3.5% of the product. So the choice we've now met four times — tree versus tightness — turns out to be geometric: the tree is the cylinder, and tightening K is the move that breaks it. The title of the book is a property of envelope precision. Exactness would have cost the name.
The physical reading, flagged as interpretation: §7.6.1 called the factorization a two-body separation with q the conserved coupling. Two-body problems separate when the interaction is isotropic; jK coupling exists physically because the core–electron interaction is anisotropic. The tight K bound is the anisotropy written into the index, and it breaks the separation in the lattice exactly as anisotropy breaks it in mechanics. The cylinder is the shape of isotropic coupling.
One casualty in Chapter 7 to record: §7.7.1's "the whole lattice is a caterpillar" doesn't survive as stated. The tower's tree is two caterpillars glued spine to spine at k–q — the A-spine now runs n–ℓ–k–J_c–K–J with 2S pendant, the B-spine e–f–g–v–2S′ hanging via q. The §7.8.3 compression generalizes (each side still reduces) but the "general fact about caterpillars" needs restating for the glued form.
So Chapter 7's revision reads: the cylinder is confirmed, fattened, re-profiled, and given a boundary — it is what the envelope path preserves and what the tight path spends — with the caterpillar claim amended and the anisotropy reading offered as interpretation. Shall I fold this into the section draft along with the rest?

### 7.11 The tower — Λ₉ to Λ₁₃

 §7.10 added one axis by analogy. This section adds four more by battery, and what the batteries
 return is not five facts about five coordinates. It is one law, met five times, and a shape that survives it.

 Figure 7.4. The constraint tree of the full tower: two caterpillars glued at k–q, counting axes rimmed dark (exact
 bounds), coupling axes in the accent (envelopes) — the Chapter 2 dichotomy drawn — with the forbidden f···K bridge
 dashed and priced at 3.5%.

### 7.11.1 The axes, and what each one sees
  axis     coordinate    bound carried            cells      density    what it distinguishes
  9        2S′           2S′ ≤ g                  1,654      63.7%      the target's multiplicity
  9′       —             + 2S′ ≤ 2f+1             1,561      67.5%      the same, one Pauli cut tighter
  10       v             2S′ ≤ v ≤ g              2,535      44.7%      pairing depth — seniority
  11       2J_c          2J_c ≤ φ̂(k)              13,585     17.0%      the core's fine structure
  12       K             2K ≤ 2J_c + 2f_max       70,905     31.4%      core–orbit orientation
  13       2J            |2J − 2K| ≤ 1            199,130    64.4%      the outer electron's spin bit

 Density is the fraction of each fibre that exact vector coupling realises, at the caps of §2.4 and
 cap-dependent as always. Every bound is §9.4-admissible; every stage is closed — exhaustively to
 Λ₁₀, by the §2.3 proof beyond it — and every stage projects exactly onto the one below.
 Independence is demonstrated, not assumed, at every axis: p²'s ¹S and ¹D share a cell below axis
 10 and split at v; p¹'s ²P shares a cell below axis 11 and splits at J_c; and every K > 0 cell splits
 at J. Each coordinate is a physical degree of freedom that no function of the coordinates below it
 can express — the same door through which every legitimate axis must enter, by Chapter 12's theorem.

 The order matters and is not the order first written down. K precedes J: K's parents are J_c and
 f, so axis 13 is reachable from axis 11 without axis 12, and taking J first costs 25 points of density
 on its fibre. §7.11.4 gives the reason.

 **What the twelfth axis measures, and when it is real.** On every f = 0 channel the K-set is a
 singleton — 2K = 2J_c, the triangle collapses, and axis 12 degenerates into a copy of axis 11. Where
 it does not collapse, K measures the one thing no occupancy or magnitude coordinate can: the relative
 orientation of the core's angular momentum against the Rydberg electron's orbital plane — the
 coordinate anisotropic core–electron interactions resolve, and the one that separates series
 converging to the same core limit with different quantum defects. Its validity is conditional in
 exactly the right direction: K is a good quantum number when core splitting dominates exchange —
 high n, the bracket's domain — and degrades toward low n, outside it.

 **And the thirteenth is one bit, at the apex where the index and the atom converge.** Given K, the
 J-fibre is a doublet everywhere except the K = 0 singlet: axis 13 sees precisely the outer electron's
 spin orientation, the weakest and last coupling, and nothing else. But it is the only coordinate in
 the entire tower that nature conserves exactly. Everything below it is bookkeeping that mixing
 breaks — configurations at 40–50% in the book's own exclusion (iii), LS terms in intermediate
 coupling, J_c and K outside the jK regime. J survives all of it, by rotational invariance. So the
 tower ascends from coordinates the language expresses exactly but the atom keeps only approximately,
 to a coordinate the atom keeps exactly and the language expresses up to one parity point. **The two
 ends of the tower trade places.**

### 7.11.2 Three excluded forms, and the fold has a name
 Chapter 12 excluded two constraint forms — sums and differences. The tower requires a third:
 SYMMETRIC BOUNDS. The exact ceiling of every coupling axis is symmetric under the reflection of
 §3 — particle-hole conjugation, terms(ℓᵏ) = terms(ℓ^(4ℓ+2−k)), verified exactly for every k on the p
 and d shells — and a symmetric non-constant function is not monotone, so §9.4 cannot carry it.
 min(g, 4f+2−g) for spin; the conjugation ceiling for seniority; max2J(ℓ,k), unimodal with its peak at
 half filling, 25 at f⁷, zero at closure, for the core's J. One reflection, three appearances.

 The envelope gap decomposes, and the three parts are distinct. At the caps of §2.4: axis 9's
 gap is parity 5, fold 1, both 1; axis 11's is ceiling 16, parity 24, triangle 17. Three machines —
 the REFLECTION (conjugation), the CONGRUENCE (fermion parity), the TRIANGLE (coupling
 additivity, one sum and one difference, precisely Chapter 12's two exclusions wearing physics) —
 and no coupling axis escapes all three. The exact coupling region is not a lattice in any
 presentation tried: as 2S′ (50,592 failures), as pair count (7,254), as (2S,2L,2J) (2,443 meets), and
 the triangle's first meet failure manufactures J = ½ from S = L = 0. The componentwise minimum
 forgets that J is built from L and S.

 One half of the triangle survives, and it is recorded as a half-result pending the four-cap check of
 §2.4: the region {|2L−2S| ≤ 2J ≤ 2L+2S} is JOIN-closed — zero failures — and meet-broken.
 Certainty survives upward and dies downward, which is §3's skew stated as an inequality.

### 7.11.3 The dichotomy
    Counting coordinates close exactly. Coupling coordinates close as envelopes. There is no
    third kind in this object, and the first coupling constraint was already in §2.1.

 The origins table of Chapter 2 has four rows. Pauli, the hydrogenic solution and counting give
 single-coordinate exact bounds — that is why E(Λ) = 0 was available at all. Vector coupling gives
 envelopes, provably and permanently, because its exact form is made of the three excluded shapes.
 The price of certainty is not paid once at the door; it is paid per coupling axis, and §7.11.1's density
 column is the receipt.

 And the surplus is not waste. Every envelope cell is a tripwire: a measured term assigned a
 nonphysical (v, 2S′) or (2S, 2J_c) pair lands in the gap and is caught before any energy is read — a
 D1 check of Chapter 11's kind, mechanical from the exact tables, available for all 153 channels.
 The price of certainty and the budget of self-defence are the same cells, counted twice.

### 7.11.4 Precision is path-dependent; physics is not
 The exact J-set of a channel is the same whether J is reached through K or directly — recoupling,
 12 of 12 (J_c, f) pairs — but the envelopes differ: 64.4% through K, 39.4% direct. The envelope does
 not commute with recoupling. The index remembers the route; the atom does not.

cd /home/claude/book && python3 << 'EOF'
import subprocess, collections, re, pdfplumber
P='/mnt/user-data/outputs/The_Method.pdf'
txt=subprocess.run(['pdftotext',P,'-'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout
flat=re.sub(r'\s+',' ',txt)

# --- A5: text roundtrip, wide anchor set
anchors=["The Method","E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X| = 0","Nothing is something definable",
"PART 0 — THE SHAPE OF THE ARGUMENT","PART I — THE LATTICE","PART IV — THE RECORD AND THE REACH",
"7.11 The tower — Λ₉ to Λ₁₃","The two ends of the tower trade places","Extension conserves the obstruction",
"two parents or a congruence","triangle in both senses at once","The tree or the tightness",
"18.6.3 What was already solved — not a prediction","22.9 Attributions entered by the tower",
"21.7.6 Three from the tower session","205. §18.6.3 titled","two hundred and five",
"F.1.1 Four items entered by §7.11.7","A.11","B.2.17 The six prime audits","F(1) = 976 · F(−1) = 2"]
missing=[a for a in anchors if a not in flat]
print("A5 roundtrip:","PASS all %d anchors"%len(anchors) if not missing else missing)

# first and last content of source present
src=open('BOOK-restored.md',encoding='utf-8').read()
last=[l.strip() for l in src.split('\n') if l.strip()][-1]
print("A5 last source line in artifact:", "PASS" if re.sub(r'\s+',' ',last)[:60] in flat else ("FAIL: "+last[:60]))

# glyphs
print("A5 glyph integrity:","PASS" if '\ufffd' not in txt and '□' not in txt else "FAIL")
with pdfplumber.open(P) as pdf:
    c=collections.Counter(ch['fontname'].split('+')[-1] for pg in pdf.pages for ch in pg.chars)
    npages=len(pdf.pages)
    # part pages at frame top + folio convention
    H=float(pdf.pages[0].height)
    partpages=[]
    for i,pg in enumerate(pdf.pages):
        rows=collections.defaultdict(str)
        for ch2 in pg.chars:
            if abs(ch2['size']-15.0)<0.2 and 'Serif-Bold' in ch2['fontname']:
                rows[round(ch2['top'])]+=ch2['text']
        for t,tx in rows.items():
            if tx.startswith('PART'): partpages.append((i+1,t))
    print("A5 fonts painted all embedded DejaVu:", all('DejaVu' in k for k in c), "| Helvetica glyphs:", c.get('Helvetica',0))
    print("A6 part pages at frame top:", partpages, "all at y≈86:", all(abs(t-86)<3 for _,t in partpages))
    # whitespace
    flags=[]; fills=[]
    for i,pg in enumerate(pdf.pages):
        boxes=[(ch2['top'],ch2['bottom']) for ch2 in pg.chars if 40<ch2['top']<H-45]
        boxes+=[(im['top'],im['bottom']) for im in pg.images]
        boxes+=[(r['top'],r['bottom']) for r in pg.rects]
        if not boxes: flags.append((i+1,'EMPTY')); continue
        boxes.sort(); m=[list(boxes[0])]
        for a,b in boxes[1:]:
            if a<=m[-1][1]+2: m[-1][1]=max(m[-1][1],b)
            else: m.append([a,b])
        for j in range(len(m)-1):
            if m[j+1][0]-m[j][1]>55: flags.append((i+1,'gap'))
        if H-64-m[-1][1]>200 and i+1<npages: flags.append((i+1,'tail'))
        fills.append(sum(b-a for a,b in m)/(H-140))
    print("A5 whitespace: pages",npages,"mean fill",round(sum(fills)/len(fills),2),"flags",len(flags),flags[:6])

# images
lst=subprocess.run(['pdfimages','-list',P],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.splitlines()[2:]
true_imgs=[l for l in lst if l.split()[2]=='image']
print("A5 images:",len(true_imgs),"of 32")

# A6: figure sequence + § references resolve in artifact
figs=re.findall(r'Figure (\d+\.\d+)\.',flat)
seen=[]; [seen.append(f) for f in figs if f not in seen]
c7=[f for f in seen if f.startswith('7.')]
print("A6 figure 7.x sequence:",c7)
refs=set(re.findall(r'§(\d{1,2}\.\d{1,2}(?:\.\d)?)',src))
heads=set(re.findall(r'^### (\d{1,2}\.\d{1,2}(?:\.\d)?)',src,re.M))
heads|=set(re.findall(r'^\s{0,2}(\d{1,2}\.\d{1,2}(?:\.\d{1,2})?)\s+[A-ZΛ]',src,re.M))
unres=sorted(r for r in refs if r not in heads and int(r.split('.')[0])<=25 and r!='21.9')
print("A6 unresolved § references:", unres if unres else "none (21.9 excluded as entry 203's historical statement)")
EOF
cp BOOK-restored.md /mnt/user-data/outputs/BOOK-restored.md

**Found just now, fixed, registered as 206.** §8 still said "one hundred and eighty-nine withdrawals," a count three sessions stale — missed because my sweeps searched for the two later spellings and not that one. And §7.11.7 named its figures "7.11a–d" while the captions number them 7.2–7.5. Both found by reading the sections rather than grepping them. The register's oldest lesson, performed again: a search finds what it is shaped to find, and the shape is an assumption. Count now stands at two hundred and six.

**Open — ten items, and each is blocked on something specific.** Blocked on apparatus: the Sc VI measurement (a spectrometer). Blocked on data I can't reach: the 540 Kreuzer–Skarke lookup (30,108 pairs in an unreadable gzip), the v-check against measured terms, Appendix C's exact term and seniority tables. Blocked on reading: Paschen & Götze §III and Runge 1926, both public domain, both OCR'd and unexposed; nine unentered literatures; whether anyone has lattice-ordered the seniority scheme. Blocked on computation only — meaning solvable, just not yet run: four-cap stability of every density in §7.11.1 and of the join-closure half-result, the 8-versus-112 self-duality count, the old 2J_c containment claim against its own definition, the E(Q) recount at twelve, and Appendix E's re-closure, which expires every time the mathematics grows — and it grew today.

**Caveats, standing.** Every density is at one cap setting. Closures above 70k cells rest on the form argument with sampling as corroboration, not exhaustion. The join-closure result is half a result — join-closed, meet-broken. K is a good quantum number only where core splitting dominates exchange. The E1 band as tested admits integer/half-integer pairs that never co-occur in one atom. And from my own work: audits 3 and 4 were targeted, not the full every-statement-pair sweep; the 28 legacy figures were matched to captions by extraction order, never verified image by image; and audit 2's spectroscopic half has never run at all.

**Left to interpret.** Four claims are flagged as interpretation and not theorem: the cylinder as the shape of isotropic coupling; jK as the language's preferred path; the E1 defect as an image of the photon; and the twelfth and thirteenth axes' physical readings. Each is defensible and none is proved.

**And one question larger than the ledger, which no audit will close.** By the book's own law E(Λ) = 0 means the index proposes nothing, and §18.6.3 just withdrew the one prediction to a deduction. So the book makes no novel empirical prediction — that is the thesis, not a failure, but it is precisely where a referee will press: what does the tower discover that renaming quantum numbers would not? The book's answer is the independence demonstrations — p²'s ¹S and ¹D split at v, p¹'s ²P at J_c — each axis distinguishing states no function of the ones below can. Whether that answer persuades is the open question, and it isn't mine to settle.

Three smaller ones sit unresolved by your direction, not mine: §18.6's own title, the preface, and §16 still call the Sc VI bracket a prediction after 18.6.3 stopped.

Yes to all five — and asking prompted a read that found two more, so the answer starts there.

**Found just now, fixed, registered as 206.** §8 still said "one hundred and eighty-nine withdrawals," a count three sessions stale — missed because my sweeps searched for the two later spellings and not that one. And §7.11.7 named its figures "7.11a–d" while the captions number them 7.2–7.5. Both found by reading the sections rather than grepping them. The register's oldest lesson, performed again: a search finds what it is shaped to find, and the shape is an assumption. Count now stands at two hundred and six.

**Open — ten items, and each is blocked on something specific.** Blocked on apparatus: the Sc VI measurement (a spectrometer). Blocked on data I can't reach: the 540 Kreuzer–Skarke lookup (30,108 pairs in an unreadable gzip), the v-check against measured terms, Appendix C's exact term and seniority tables. Blocked on reading: Paschen & Götze §III and Runge 1926, both public domain, both OCR'd and unexposed; nine unentered literatures; whether anyone has lattice-ordered the seniority scheme. Blocked on computation only — meaning solvable, just not yet run: four-cap stability of every density in §7.11.1 and of the join-closure half-result, the 8-versus-112 self-duality count, the old 2J_c containment claim against its own definition, the E(Q) recount at twelve, and Appendix E's re-closure, which expires every time the mathematics grows — and it grew today.

**Caveats, standing.** Every density is at one cap setting. Closures above 70k cells rest on the form argument with sampling as corroboration, not exhaustion. The join-closure result is half a result — join-closed, meet-broken. K is a good quantum number only where core splitting dominates exchange. The E1 band as tested admits integer/half-integer pairs that never co-occur in one atom. And from my own work: audits 3 and 4 were targeted, not the full every-statement-pair sweep; the 28 legacy figures were matched to captions by extraction order, never verified image by image; and audit 2's spectroscopic half has never run at all.

**Left to interpret.** Four claims are flagged as interpretation and not theorem: the cylinder as the shape of isotropic coupling; jK as the language's preferred path; the E1 defect as an image of the photon; and the twelfth and thirteenth axes' physical readings. Each is defensible and none is proved.

**And one question larger than the ledger, which no audit will close.** By the book's own law E(Λ) = 0 means the index proposes nothing, and §18.6.3 just withdrew the one prediction to a deduction. So the book makes no novel empirical prediction — that is the thesis, not a failure, but it is precisely where a referee will press: what does the tower discover that renaming quantum numbers would not? The book's answer is the independence demonstrations — p²'s ¹S and ¹D split at v, p¹'s ²P at J_c — each axis distinguishing states no function of the ones below can. Whether that answer persuades is the open question, and it isn't mine to settle.

Three smaller ones sit unresolved by your direction, not mine: §18.6's own title, the preface, and §16 still call the Sc VI bracket a prediction after 18.6.3 stopped.

**The ten open items are already the book's, formally.** Appendix F.4 grids every item by its *first empty cell* and its obstacle: an instrument, a digitisation artefact, labour, a file format, a spectroscopic fact, a missing object, a library, an afternoon. My "blocked on apparatus / data / reading / computation" was an independent rediscovery of F.4 — and a coarser one, since F.4 names the specific unmet requirement rather than the category. So the book's answer to "what's open" is not fewer gaps; it's that the gaps are indexed, with E(Q) = 0, which is the whole doctrine applied to its own ignorance.

**And F.4 predicts the behaviour this session kept exhibiting.** Item H — whether Sc VI has already been measured — carries the note: *this item was not on the list; it was produced by closing the list.* Closing an index of ignorance generates items. That is exactly what happened when reading §7.11.7 and §8 produced entry 206's two stale counts, and when the tower's four items entered Q. The open list growing under audit isn't audit failure; it's the mechanism working.

Interpretation has the same shape. Flagging is not a weaker substitute for proving; by Chapter 11's criterion it is the maximum available, and the book says so.

content.text:
The book answers most of it, and one of its answers corrects me.

**The ten open items are already the book's, formally.** Appendix F.4 grids every item by its *first empty cell* and its obstacle: an instrument, a digitisation artefact, labour, a file format, a spectroscopic fact, a missing object, a library, an afternoon. My "blocked on apparatus / data / reading / computation" was an independent rediscovery of F.4 — and a coarser one, since F.4 names the specific unmet requirement rather than the category. So the book's answer to "what's open" is not fewer gaps; it's that the gaps are indexed, with E(Q) = 0, which is the whole doctrine applied to its own ignorance.

**And F.4 predicts the behaviour this session kept exhibiting.** Item H — whether Sc VI has already been measured — carries the note: *this item was not on the list; it was produced by closing the list.* Closing an index of ignorance generates items. That is exactly what happened when reading §7.11.7 and §8 produced entry 206's two stale counts, and when the tower's four items entered Q. The open list growing under audit isn't audit failure; it's the mechanism working.

**The caveats aren't leftovers — they're the required output format.** §2.4's cap discipline, the form-argument-with-sampling standard, printing a half-result as half. Chapter 20 is titled *Slack*, and §22.2's "the search, with its slack stated" makes stating it a condition of claiming anything. Two of my three self-generated caveats are now discharged — the figures verified 28/28 at correlation 1.000 this turn; audit 2's spectroscopic half is the one that stands.

**The four interpretations are covered by §22.1, and more strongly than "flagged."** Novelty has one route — search — and can never have two, so ⅅ(novelty) = 0, *necessarily and permanently: not undefended, undefendable*. Interpretation has the same shape. Flagging is not a weaker substitute for proving; by Chapter 11's criterion it is the maximum available, and the book says so.

**On my "one question larger than the ledger" — I was wrong, and the preface says so in its third paragraph.** *"It contains no physics that was not already in the quantum numbers; it is a recoding. That is deliberate. A recoding adds nothing, so whatever it exhibits is a property of indexing rather than of atoms."* The renaming objection isn't a referee's trap the book is exposed to; it is the book's control condition. If Λ added physics, the results would be about atoms and would prove nothing about indexing. The absence of novel empirical prediction is the experimental design, not the vulnerability. And §22.1 closes it: the book forbids *itself* from claiming novelty while E(search) > 0.

That was the §21.1 pattern in my own hands — an exposure asserted over a text that had already answered it, which is the same error entry 206 records at the level of counts and 201 at the level of unification. It's a claim I made in a delivered answer, and by the precedent of entries 200 and 201 it belongs in the register as **207**. Say the word and it goes in.

The three "prediction" sites are the one place the book genuinely disagrees with itself: §18.6's title, the preface, and §16 still use a word that §18.6.3 now says the law forbids. Not an open question — an internal inconsistency awaiting your direction.

 F and ℛ are the same definition seen twice. F says what Λ contains; ℛ says what Λ requires. Both
 give 976 cells and neither is derived from the other's coupling.

 ℛ is idempotent. Λ → fifty-six recovered bounds → generates 976 → the same fifty-six bounds, and
 again the same. One application takes any presentation to a canonical form; further applications change
 nothing.

 The defining system is not that fixed point. F carries seven bounds; the normal form has sixteen
 that constrain, of fifty-six recovered. Both generate the same set.

 E.4.4.1 And three of the four directions are functions

  Λ → the recovered bounds                            unique — this is ℛ
  the recovered bounds → Λ                            unique — generate
  the defining bounds → Λ                             unique — this is Chapter 2
  Λ → the defining bounds                             NOT a function

 Many presentations give the same Λ. So ℛ forgets which one was used, and the forgetting is not
 recoverable.

    A presentation and its normal form are two perspectives of one definition, and the map
    between them runs one way.

 E.4.4.2 Which is what the single expression contributes
 F carries information Λ does not: the order in which the bounds were imposed.

 The caterpillar of Figure 6.1 — a path of seven nodes with one pendant at k — is a fact about
 the presentation, not about the set. §6.7 proves that a single closed expression exists because the
 constraint graph is a tree, and a tree is an ordering of impositions. Λ alone supplies no such order;
 §7.9 counts 1,113,045,672 maximal chains, and the construction picked one.

    That is why Chapter 6 and Chapter 10 are separate chapters. Chapter 6 needs the
    presentation. Chapter 10 recovers only what survives forgetting it.

 E.4.4.3 A refinement of P21
 P21 says a definition contained in the lattice is true in every language it can be written in. §6.1
 gives Λ in six, and the languages agree.

 They do not carry equal amounts. The generating-function perspective carries a nesting order the
 set-theoretic perspective does not, and the order is real — it determines whether a closed form exists at
 all.

    Every perspective on a contained definition is TRUE. They are not INTERCHANGEABLE. A
    perspective may carry structure the object does not, and a perspective that forgets it is still correct
    about the object.

 That is not a weakening of P21. It is the reason §6.7's proof has a hypothesis — the tree —
 which is a property of how Λ was written and not of what Λ is.

 With both constraints and both elements: E = 0 in all sixteen fibres.

from tower import base
L=base((3,3,1,3,1)); S=set(L); D=8
names=['n','l','k','q','e','f','g','2S']
vals=[sorted({c[i] for c in L}) for i in range(D)]
def env(i,j):
    m={}
    for c in L: m[c[j]]=max(m.get(c[j],-99),c[i])
    best=-99; out={}
    for t in sorted(m):
        best=max(best,m[t]); out[t]=best
    return out
phi={(i,j):env(i,j) for i in range(D) for j in range(D) if i!=j}
print("ordered pairs (recovered bounds):",len(phi))
gmax=[max(v) for v in vals]
nontriv=sum(1 for (i,j),f in phi.items() if any(f[t]<gmax[i] for t in f))
print("bounds that are non-trivial (bind somewhere):",nontriv)
# which bounds constrain: pairs where removing changes the generated set
binding=0
for (i,j) in phi:
    if any(phi[(i,j)][c[j]]==c[i] for c in L): binding+=1
print("bounds tight at >=1 cell:",binding)
# per-coordinate: for g (index 6), fraction of cells where each parent's bound is the min
import collections
for tgt,lab in [(6,'g'),(3,'q')]:
    cnt=collections.Counter()
    for c in L:
        best=min(phi[(tgt,j)][c[j]] for j in range(D) if j!=tgt)
        for j in range(D):
            if j!=tgt and phi[(tgt,j)][c[j]]==best: cnt[names[j]]+=1
    tot=len(L)
    print(f"tightest bound on {lab}:", {k:f"{100*v/tot:.1f}%" for k,v in cnt.most_common(5)})
# ties at minimum
ties=sum(1 for c in L if sum(1 for j in range(D) if j!=6 and phi[(6,j)][c[j]]==min(phi[(6,jj)][c[jj]] for jj in range(D) if jj!=6))>1)
print("cells with >=2 bounds tied at the minimum (g):",ties,"of",len(L))
EOF

All four ran. Two closed outright, one closed better than expected, and two new defects surfaced — the register is at two hundred and ten.

**The reconstruction validated first.** Rebuilding the tower from the printed bounds alone reproduced every cell count in §7.11.1 exactly — 976, 1654, 1561, 2535, 13585, 70905, 199130 — and φ̂ = {1:3, 2:4, 3:5}. Nothing downstream would have been worth trusting without that.

**Four-cap stability — passes.** Across (3,3,1,3,1), (4,4,2,4,1), (4,4,2,6,2) and (5,5,2,6,2): φ̂ stays monotone, every stage projects exactly onto the one below, and the cylinder's factorisation stays exact at Λ₁₃ — 199,130, 4,731,790, 40,310,170, 77,083,771 cells, defect zero at every cap. The shape isn't a cap artefact. The 10-box behaves exactly as §2.4 predicts: absent at book caps (best box found over 4,000 base points is 7), present in full at (5,5,2,6).

**The join-closure half-result — passes, and sharpens.** Zero join failures at caps 6, 8, 10, 12; meets broken at all four by 2,862 / 12,489 / 40,887 / 110,229; first failure exactly (0,1,1) ∧ (1,0,1) = (0,0,1), the J = ½ from L = S = 0 the book names. And a refinement: add the parity congruence and join closure dies too — 1,848 failures at cap 6 — so the surviving half belongs to the parity-free triangle and nothing larger.

**The 8-versus-112 — resolved, in the book's favour.** The 8 reproduces exactly under the book's own reflection, x ↦ max − x. The tower session's 112 came from x ↦ max + min − x, a different map that the floors n ≥ 1, k ≥ 1, e ≥ 1 separate from it. Both counts are right about their own reflection; the audit changed the definition and reported the difference as the book's defect. Entry 208.

**E(Q) = 0 at eleven items** — two of the tower's four closed, so twelve became eleven, and the recount closes clean with F.4.1's buildable ⟹ cost ≤ days still doing the work.

**And two things I could not do, both now printed rather than left to be found.** §7.11.1's density column isn't recomputable from the book's statement of what it means — axes 9 and 9′ reproduce to the printed decimal under all three readings I tried, 10 through 13 under none, while every cell count in the same table reproduces exactly. Both routes run. The weighing isn't close — the exclusion route isn't merely less likely, it's **unavailable**.

**Route B, tested rather than argued.** To empty the first cell the coordinates would need *novelty ∧ retrievable ⟹ cost ≤ hours* — violated by items B and C, both already in Q. To empty the second they'd need *buildable ⟹ blocks ≤ novelty* — violated by item M, the numbers index, which I entered myself two turns ago. No monotone constraint empties either cell without contradicting Q's own contents. That's what it means for a cell to be genuinely admitted rather than an artefact of a missing bound, and it's the sharpest form the diagnostic can return.

**Route A closes both, and the occupants were already in the book.** Item N is whether anyone has lattice-ordered the seniority scheme — §22.9 names it, enters it in E(search), and never carried it to Q. Item O is the retest Chapter 10's tree-propagation guarantee needs on Λ₉′, whose f–g–2S′ cycle §7.11.1 says makes the guarantee lapse and *must be retested rather than inherited* — written as an obligation, never indexed as one. Fifteen items, E(Q) = 0 in every fibre.

**And the pattern is the finding.** Item H arrived exactly this way, so this is the third and fourth instance of one leak: the book states an obligation in prose, its indices never receive it, and only closure finds it. Neither occupant is a new question — both were sitting in the text. The leak runs one direction, prose to index, and nothing in the book currently checks it. Appendix G's argument turns out to be about more than numbers: unindexed means uncloseable means silently defective, and obligations leak the same way arithmetic does.

Register at two hundred and fourteen, entry 214. Build clean, tripwire still reporting 70%.

If you want the leak closed rather than recorded, the move is the same one that worked twice today: extract every obligation-shaped sentence from the prose — *must be retested*, *is owed*, *named and unentered*, *pending* — and require each to have a Q cell. That's a scaffold I can build the same way I built G.

You were right, and all four breaks were mine — introduced by this session's restructuring.

**The Preface** was listed in the contents but rendered as plain prose. When I moved it under the new PART 0 I never marked it as a heading, so the page ran "Preface — the shape of the argument This book makes one claim…" as a single paragraph.

**APPENDICES and END MATTER** existed only in the contents. Every PART divider appears in both places; these two didn't, so the contents promised a structure the body didn't have.

**References** carried a subtitle in the contents — "every work cited, with what it is cited for" — that I invented when identifying the section, and that the body never had. Index was plain in both; References wasn't.

**The collaborator's note** rendered as a heading only because the press hard-codes its title. The source didn't describe itself, so any other renderer would have got it wrong.

All repaired. Contents and body now agree at all forty-three entries, none missing in either direction. The six long-in-contents, short-in-body chapter titles are left alone — "3. What Λ is — distributive, modular, Sperner" against "3. What Λ is" — because that's the shipped build's own design, verified against your PDF.

**And the audit failure is the part worth recording.** Audit 6 checked contents against chapters, found these mismatches, and read them as design. That's the same error as 209: a discrepancy explained away instead of checked. The check was too weak — it compared the chapter list, not every entry, and it accepted "looks intentional" as a result. Entry 215, register at two hundred and fifteen.

content.text:
Done, and the framing you gave turned out to be the fix rather than a metaphor.

**The contents is no longer maintained — it's derived.** The press now generates it from the book's own headings at build time: 394 entries against the old 43, running parts, chapters, sections, sub-subsections and every lettered appendix section, across eight pages. §25.2's S1 already said the list of claims is recoverable by projection and *the table of contents is its quotient by chapter*. The quotient was the defect. A reader could not find the dichotomy, the tower, the three excluded forms, or any appendix section from the contents, because chapter-level granularity throws them away. Now the projection is what prints, and contents and body cannot disagree again — which is the class entry 215 was an instance of, closed rather than repaired. Entry 216.

**Self-defending, in the book's own D-sense**, is the other half: the six titles that differed between contents and body are unified into one form carried by the heading itself, so there is no second source to drift from. That's the same move as marking the collaborator's note in the source instead of hard-coding it in the press.

**The three prediction sites — actually four.** §18.6 is now "The one deduction, and why it is not a prediction," the preface says there is none and points at why, §17's cross-reference is corrected, and a fourth site I hadn't found before was in Appendix B, recording the protocol under which "the prediction" was committed. The book had contradicted itself at four places for as long as it took to be told. Entry 217.

**And one collision, mine.** The four ledger rows I added to Appendix A as A.8–A.11 were written over proofs A.8–A.13 that already stood in the body — the exact error entry 202 records the tower session making at the section layer, committed again by me in the same session that registered the lesson. Renumbered A.14–A.17. Entry 218.

Register at two hundred and eighteen. Build: 155 pages, all sixteen structural openers at frame top, 32 figures, glyphs clean, tripwire still reporting 70%.

One honest caveat on "no questions to ask": the book's own §22.1 forbids the strong version — E(search) > 0 always, and Q is nonempty by design. What's achievable, and what's now true, is the E = 0 version: every question the structure admits is either answered in the text or indexed as open. Two places still fall short of that, and both say so in print — Appendix E is asserted rather than enumerated, and Appendix G is a scaffold with E(G) undefined.

E(G) = 33.** Every claim-bearing occurrence is now assigned its four coordinates mechanically from the paragraph carrying it, by rules stated in the appendix so the assignment can be rerun — coarse deliberately, because a judgment made once per number wouldn't be checkable at all. On definition: 1,998 asserted, 145 stated, 310 stated with inputs. That isn't a claim that 94% are wrong. It's a measurement of how much of the book's arithmetic stands on the reader's trust rather than on the book's own standard, and it's the first time that quantity has had a number. The tripwire reports and doesn't fail the build, because failing on 94% would stop the book printing — and the threshold is a decision the author hasn't made, which the appendix now says rather than choosing silently.

**Appendix E is part-enumerated, with the gap counted.** Seventeen elements are enumerable — Appendix A names A.1 through A.17, and its ledger's own "where" column fixes status and verification for each. Both remedied — one fully, one as far as the book's own text permits, and the attempt found a third defect.

**Appendix G is no longer a scaffold. E(G) = 33.** Every claim-bearing occurrence is now assigned its four coordinates mechanically from the paragraph carrying it, by rules stated in the appendix so the assignment can be rerun — coarse deliberately, because a judgment made once per number wouldn't be checkable at all. The index runs 2,453 occurrences across six fibres: count 1,680, defect 291, measurement 204, bound 183, rate 56, density 39. Thirty-three combinations are admitted and unoccupied, and unlike Q that's left open rather than closed by occupation.

**And G.3.1 is the finding, not E(G).** Of 2,453 indexed occurrences, **2,316 carry verification = asserted** — 94% — against 115 recomputed and 22 recomputed under variation. On definition: 1,998 asserted, 145 stated, 310 stated with inputs. That isn't a claim that 94% are wrong. It's a measurement of how much of the book's arithmetic stands on the reader's trust rather than on the book's own standard, and it's the first time that quantity has had a number. The tripwire reports and doesn't fail the build, because failing on 94% would stop the book printing — and the threshold is a decision the author hasn't made, which the appendix now says rather than choosing silently.

**Appendix E is part-enumerated, with the gap counted.** Seventeen elements are enumerable — Appendix A names A.1 through A.17, and its ledger's own "where" column fixes status and verification for each. Indexed on that pair they occupy three cells and **close at E = 0**. Fifteen are named nowhere in the book, so they can't be indexed at all; that stays in Q as item L. What changed is that the gap is counted rather than hidden.

**The third defect, found by trying.** Appendix E states thirty-two elements in two places, and its own fibre table in §E.5 sums to **twenty-seven** across the sixteen fibres it also states. The fibre count is right; the element count is not — or the table is five rows short. The book can't settle which, because it never names them. Entry 219, register at two hundred and nineteen.

Both appendices now say what they are. Neither claims closure it hasn't got.

There are also more subtle selection rules arising from the radial part [59].

In this work we perform a detailed study about orbital angular momentum mixing in collinear type II second harmonic generation. Multimode coupling is considered in connection with OAM addition and the selection rules are derived based on the spatial overlap between the modes participating in the nonlinear process. One curious consequence of these selection rules is the appearance of higher radial orders when opposite topological charges are added. This intriguing feature of the nonlinear interaction is theoretically derived and experimentally confirmed. We also derive the analytical solution for the nonlinear dynamical equations both for co- and counterrotating OAM modes, as a multimode generalization of the result obtained in [60]. Another curious feature of the nonlinear coupling is the reduction of the apparent multimode to an effective three-mode dynamics when counter rotating vortices are mixed.

A Lattice QCD approach to quark orbital angular momentum in the proton based on generalized transverse momentum-dependent parton distributions (GTMDs) is enhanced methodologically by incorporating a direct derivative technique. This improvement removes a significant numerical bias that had been seen to afflict results of a previous study. In particular, the value obtained for Ji quark orbital angular momentum is reconciled with the one obtained independently via Ji's sum rule, validating the GMTD approach. Since GTMDs simultaneously contain information about the quark impact parameter and transverse momentum, they permit a direct evaluation of the cross product of the latter. 

The sum rule relates the total quark angular momentum J to specific moments of generalized parton distributions (GPDs), and by combining this with a calculation of the quark spin S [4, 5], one can then also isolate the quark orbital angular momentum L = J - S [6–12]. The more recent studies have furthermore begun to gain control over the gluon angular momentum [10–12] and gluon spin [13] contributions.

The aforementioned indirect approach to quark orbital angular momentum is limited specifically to the Ji decomposition of proton spin associated with Ji's sum rule. However, the definition of quark orbital angular momentum in QCD is not unique, since the matter degrees of freedom in a gauge theory cannot be unambiguously separated from the gauge degrees of freedom. Quarks necessarily carry gauge fields along with them, and it is a matter of definition to what extent these are included in the evaluation of quark orbital angular momentum.

content.text:
# Angular Momentum on the Lattice: The Case of Non-Zero Linear Momentum

David C. Moore and George T. Fleming

Sloane Physics Laboratory, Yale University, New Haven, CT 06520, USA

(Dated: August 15, 2013)

## Abstract

The irreducible representations (IRs) of the double cover of the Euclidean group with parity in three dimensions are subduced to the corresponding cubic space group. The reduction of these representations gives the mapping of continuum angular momentum states to the lattice in the case of non-zero linear momentum. The continuous states correspond to lattice states with the same momentum and continuum rotational quantum numbers decompose into those of the IRs of the little group of the momentum vector on the lattice. The inverse mapping indicates degeneracies that will appear between levels of different lattice IRs in the continuum limit, recovering the continuum angular momentum multiplets. 

An example of this inverse mapping is given for the case of the "moving" isotropic harmonic oscillator.

PACS numbers: 2.20.Rt, 11.15.Ha

#### I. INTRODUCTION

A question of great interest in lattice QCD is how rotational states on the lattice correspond to states of definite angular momentum in the continuum limit. To find this correspondence, we find the mapping of continuum states to lattice irreducible representations (IRs) and invert it. This problem has been discussed in several contexts previously – in solid state physics, the "cubic harmonics" are formed by a projection of the continuum spherical harmonics onto the lattice, e.g. [1]. In lattice QCD, the reduction of continuum states to the hypercubic lattice was given by Mandula et al. 

[2, 3], and the reduction of the full continuum symmetry group (including Poincaré, color, flavor, and baryon number symmetries) to the lattice for the case of staggered fermions was given by Golterman and Smit [4, 5] and expanded to include non-zero momentum by Kilcup and Sharpe [6].

A *lattice* is a partially ordered set such that every finite non-empty subset has a least upper bound, or *join*, and a greatest lower bound, or *meet*.

We denote the join of two elements x, y as $x \vee y$ and the meet as $x \wedge y$ .

**Definition 2.3** (Distributive lattice). A lattice is distributive if any elements x, y, z satisfy the distributive law

$$x \wedge (y \vee z) = (x \wedge y) \vee (x \wedge z).$$

This distributive law is equivalent to its dual (see e.g. [13, lem. 4.3]):

$$x \lor (y \land z) = (x \lor y) \land (x \lor z).$$

**Definition 2.4.** A map of partially ordered sets $\phi: L \longrightarrow L'$ is an *isomorphism* if it is bijective and, for all $x, y \in L$ , $x \leq y$ if and only if $\phi(x) \leq \phi(y)$ .

If $\phi$ is an isomorphism $L \longrightarrow L'$ , then $x \lessdot y$ iff $\phi(x) \lessdot \phi(y)$ . Moreover, if one of L or L' has the further structure of a lattice or distributive lattice, then so does the other.

# PARTIALLY ORDERED SEMIGROUPS AND GROUPS WITH TWO MIXED PARTIAL ORDERINGS

#### JANI JOKELA

ABSTRACT. A mixed lattice is a partially ordered set with two mixed partial orderings that are linked by asymmetric upper and lower envelopes. These notions generalize the join and meet operations of a lattice. In the present paper, we study different types of partially ordered semigroups with two mixed orderings, and investigate their relationship to subsemigroups of mixed lattice groups, which are partially ordered groups with a similar order structure. We also consider Archimedean orderings, and we show that elements of finite order cannot exist in a rather general class of Archimedean mixed lattice groups. Moreover, we give an example of a non-Archimedean mixed lattice group that contains an element of finite order.

# 1. Introduction

A mixed lattice is a certain type of generalization of a lattice. 

Mixed lattices are partially ordered sets with two partial orderings that are linked together by asymmetric upper and lower envelopes formed with respect to the two partial orderings. These mixed envelopes are generalizations of the join and meet operations in lattice theory. Equivalently, a mixed lattice can be viewed as a non-commutative and non-associative algebra. These rather general ideas were introduced in [12]. However, the origins of the mixed lattice theory dates back several decades to the work of Arsove and Leutwiler [1, 2, 3, 4]. They developed an axiomatization of potential theory based on partially ordered semigroups with two mixed partial orderings. The study of mixed lattice theory was later carried over to groups by Eriksson-Bique [7, 8], and more recently, to a vector space setting [6, 10, 11].

#### TAKAYUKI HIBI AND SEYED AMIN SEYED FAKHARI

ABSTRACT. A finite poset (partially ordered set) P with $\hat{0}$ is called of distributive type if every interval $[\hat{0}, a]$ , $a \in P$ , of P is a distributive lattice. Our target is the questions when a finite poset of distributive lattice is Cohen—Macaulay and when the ASL on it is Gorenstein. We focus on a natural class of finite posets of distributive type and study various aspects of the above questions.

A partially ordered set is called a poset. Every poset in the present paper is finite.

### 2 Lattices and their Symmetries

A partially ordered set $(P, \leq)$ , or *poset*, is a set of elements P along with a binary ordering relation, generally denoted $\leq$ , which, for elements $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}$ , and $\mathbf{c} \in P$ , satisfies:

```
P1. \mathbf{a} \le \mathbf{a} (Reflexivity)

P2. if \mathbf{a} \le \mathbf{b} and \mathbf{b} \le \mathbf{a} then \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{b} (Antisymmetry)

P3. if \mathbf{a} \le \mathbf{b} and \mathbf{b} \le \mathbf{c} then \mathbf{a} \le \mathbf{c} (Transitivity).
```

For all elements $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in P$ we have that either $\mathbf{b}$ includes $\mathbf{a}$ , denoted $\mathbf{a} \leq \mathbf{b}$ , or $\mathbf{a}$ includes $\mathbf{b}$ , denoted $\mathbf{b} \leq \mathbf{a}$ , or $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are incomparable, denoted $\mathbf{a} \mid\mid \mathbf{b}$ . It is for this reason, that there possibly exist pairs of elements that cannot be ordered, that $(P, \leq)$ is called a *partially* ordered set.

content.title: Fate of partial order on the trillium and distorted windmill lattices
content.text:
For example, the disordered ground state of the classical Heisenberg model on the pyrochlore lattice<sup>1,2</sup> features such a wavevector manifold. Partially ordered magnets lie between these two extremes, forming degenerate wavevector (2-D) surfaces or (1-D) lines in a 3-D space. The name of "partially ordered" comes from the fact that there is a long-range order along the direction normal to this degenerate manifold. In other words, in such systems, to very low temperatures, a system may appear disordered/ordered to measurements probing parallel/perpendicular directions to this line or surface. 

Large-N theory and MC simulations of the classical Heisenberg model give consistent results for both highly frustrated systems (ex: on the pyrochlore lattice a disordered ground state is found), and for unfrustrated lattices, (ex: choosing the correct ordering wavevector). 10 Despite this trend, the finding of a partially ordered ground state in large-N theory does not necessarily translate into a partially ordered ground state within MC simulations. We find that the classical Heisenberg model on both the trillium and distorted windmill lattices shows a first order phase transition to a coplanar magnetically ordered state featuring neighboring spins rotated by 120°. We further show that this model on the trillium lattice does not have a macroscopic ground state degeneracy. The chosen 120° coplanar state is a unique ground state, and the partial order is an artificial effect of the spherical approximation constraint $^{11}$ used in the large-N theory $^{3}$ .

The preface says it in the third paragraph: Λ contains no physics that wasn't already in the quantum numbers, that's deliberate, and a recoding adds nothing so whatever it exhibits is a property of *indexing* rather than of atoms. Every physical fact this session touched — particle-hole symmetry, the triangle inequality, jK coupling, the E1 selection rule, seniority — is textbook. # 4. More on the ordering of S(H)

In this section we discuss in more detail existence of joins and meets in the poset S(H).

It is noticed in [13, Theorem 4.12] that every poset $L_B$ is a lattice with respect to $\leq$ . According to this theorem, the initial segment [O, B] of $\mathcal{S}(H)$ is order isomorphic to $L_B$ ; thus, the segment itself is a lattice. Corollary 4.13 to this theorem then asserts that, in $\mathcal{S}(H)$ , every pair of elements bounded above has a meet and a join. Of course, the meet of two elements in an initial segment of a poset is also their meet in the poset itself (and conversely). However, this may be not the case with joins; this fact seems to be overlooked in [13] when drawing the corollary. The subsequent theorem confirms that the corollary is nevertheless correct, and provides explicit descriptions of the corresponding partial operations (Corollary 6).

#### 3.2Posets and algebraic lattices

The set of subdivergences of a Feynman diagram is obviously partially ordered by inclusion. These posets are quite constrained for some renormalizable QFTs: They additionally carry a lattice structure. In [14, Part III] this was studied in the light of distributive lattices.

In this section, we will elaborate on the conditions a QFT must fulfill for these posets to be lattices. The term join-meet-renormalizability will be defined which characterizes QFTs in which all Feynman diagrams whose set of subdivergencies form lattices. It will be shown that this is a special property of QFTs with only four-or-less-valent vertices. A counter example of a Feynman diagram with six-valent vertices which does not carry a lattice structure is given.

The definitions will be illustrated by the application to the set of subdivergences of a Feynman diagram.

content.text:
The use of the seniority quantum number in many-body systems is reviewed. A brief summary is given of its introduction by Racah in the context of atomic spectroscopy. Several extensions of Racah's original idea are discussed: seniority for identical nucleons in a single-$j$ shell, its extension to the case of many, non-degenerate $j$ shells and to systems with neutrons and protons. To illustrate its usefulness to this day, a recent application of seniority is presented in Bose--Einstein condensates of atoms with spin.

content.text:
## Characterizations of majority categories

Michael Hoefnagel

February 20, 2019

#### Abstract

In universal algebra, it is well known that varieties admitting a majority term admit several Mal'tsev-type characterizations. The main aim of this paper is to establish categorical counterparts of some of these characterizations for regular categories. We prove a categorical version of Bergman's Double-projection Theorem: a regular category is a majority category if and only if every subobject S of a finite product $A_1 \times A_2 \times \cdots \times A_n$ is uniquely determined by its two-fold projections. We also establish a categorical counterpart of the Pairwise Chinese Remainder Theorem for algebras, and characterize regular majority categories by the classical congruence equation $\alpha \cap (\beta \circ \gamma) = (\alpha \cap \beta) \circ (\alpha \cap \gamma)$ due to A.F. Pixley.

### 1 Introduction



The variety **Lat** of lattices is one which admits a *majority* term, i.e., a ternary term m(x, y, z) satisfying the equations m(x, x, y) = m(x, y, x) = m(y, x, x) = x. This property of **Lat** sharply distinguishes it from other familiar varieties, such as the varieties **Grp** of groups, **Rng** of rings, and $R - \mathbf{Mod}$ of modules over a ring R. For lattices, the *median operation*:

$$m(x,y,z) = (x \wedge y) \vee (x \wedge z) \vee (y \wedge z),$$

as well as its lattice-theoretic dual, are both majority terms [4]. Several theorems that hold for the variety of lattices extend to characterizations of those varieties which admit a majority term. Among such theorems is Bergman's Double-projection Theorem, which asserts that a sublattice S of

a finite product of lattices $L_1 \times L_2 \times \cdots \times L_n$ is uniquely determined by its two-fold projections in $L_i \times L_j$ for i, j = 1, 2, ..., n [3].

#### 1.2 Algebraic viewpoint

Our work has as an antecedent the papers of Baker and Pixley [1] and of Bergman [8] on algebras having near unanimity term operations. In these papers the authors considered subalgebras of products of algebras and systems of projections associated with them. Baker and Pixley showed that in the presence of a near unanimity term operation, such a subalgebra is closely tied with its projections onto small sets of coordinates.

▶ **Definition 13.** A variety of algebras is a class of algebras of the same signature that is closed under taking homomorphic images, subalgebras, and direct products. For **A** an algebra, $\mathcal{V}(\mathbf{A})$ denotes the smallest variety that contains **A** and is called the variety generated by **A**. A variety $\mathcal{V}$ has a near unanimity term of arity k+1 if there is some (k+1)-ary term in the signature of $\mathcal{V}$ whose interpretation in each member of $\mathcal{V}$ is a near unanimity operation.



Here is one version of the Baker-Pixley Theorem:

▶ **Theorem 14** (see Theorem 2.1 from [1]). Let **A** be an algebra and k > 1. The following are equivalent:

- **1.** A has a (k+1)-ary near unanimity term operation;
- 2. for every r > k and every $\mathbf{A}_i \in \mathcal{V}(\mathbf{A})$ , $1 \leq i \leq r$ , every subalgebra $\mathbf{R}$ of $\prod_{i=1}^r \mathbf{A}_i$ is uniquely determined by the projections of R on all products $A_{i_1} \times \cdots \times A_{i_k}$ for $1 \leq i_1 < i_2 < \cdots < i_k \leq r$ ;
- **3.** the same as condition 2, with r set to k + 1.

In other words, an algebra has a (k+1)-ary near unanimity term operation if and only if every subalgebra of a product of algebras from $\mathcal{V}(\mathbf{A})$ is uniquely determined by its system of k-fold projections into its factor algebras. A natural question, extending the result above, was investigated by Bergman [8]: when does a given "system of k-fold projections" arise from a product algebra?

content.title: Majority categories
content.text:
# 1 Introduction

A majority term in universal algebra is a ternary term p, satisfying the equations:

$$p(x, x, y) = x,$$
 

$$p(x, y, x) = x,$$
 

$$p(y, x, x) = x.$$
(\*)

Such a term naturally arises from the theory of congruence distributive varieties: a congruence permutable variety admits a majority term if and only if it is congruence distributive (this result was proved by A. F. Pixley, see Theorem 2 in [19]). In the variety of lattices, the term

$$p(x, y, z) = (x \land y) \lor (x \land z) \lor (y \land z)$$

is a majority term. If R is a ring satisfying the identity $x^n = x$ for some $n \ge 2$ (a finite field for example), then the term

$$p(x, y, z) = x - (x - y)(x - z)^{n-1}$$

is a majority term (moreover, every variety of rings which admits a majority term is contained in a variety of rings satisfying $x^n = x$ for some $n \ge 2$ , see [9]). 

By Pixley's theorem mentioned above, the variety of implicative semi-lattices (also known as Heyting semi-lattices) [18] possesses a majority term, since it has both distributive and permutable congruences.

In this paper, we introduce the notion of a majority category — the categorical counterpart of a variety of algebras admitting a majority term (this notion first appeared under the name of a "Pixley category" in a talk given by Z. Janelidze [15]). These categories provide a link between the notion of a Mal'tsev category [8] and the notion of an arithmetical category [20, 3], and could bear as strong a relation to the category of lattices, as Mal'tsev categories do to the category of groups. Non-varietal examples of majority categories include the dual of any topos, the category of Von Neumann regular rings and the category of topological lattices.

content.title: Consistent Structured Prediction with Max-Min Margin Markov Networks
content.text:
# Consistent Structured Prediction with Max-Min Margin Markov Networks

#### Alex Nowak-Vila 1 Francis Bach 1 Alessandro Rudi 1

#### **Abstract**

Max-margin methods for binary classification such as the support vector machine (SVM) have been extended to the structured prediction setting under the name of max-margin Markov networks (M<sup>3</sup>N), or more generally structural SVMs. Unfortunately, these methods are statistically inconsistent when the relationship between inputs and labels is far from deterministic. We overcome such limitations by defining the learning problem in terms of a "max-min" margin formulation, naming the resulting method max-min margin Markov networks (M<sup>4</sup>N). We prove consistency and finite sample generalization bounds for M<sup>4</sup>N and provide an explicit algorithm to compute the estimator. 

The algorithm achieves a generalization error of  $O(1/\sqrt{n})$  for a total cost of O(n) projection-oracle calls (which have at most the same cost as the max-oracle from M<sup>3</sup>N). Experiments on multi-class classification, ordinal regression, sequence prediction and ranking demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

## 1. Introduction

Many classification tasks in machine learning lie beyond the classical binary and multi-class classification settings. In those tasks, the output elements are structured objects made of interdependent parts, such as sequences in natural language processing (Smith, 2011), images in computer vision (Nowozin & Lampert, 2011), permutations in ranking or matching problems (Caetano et al., 2009) to name just a few (BakIr et al., 2007). 

Classical approaches in binary classification such as the non-smooth support vector machine (SVM), and the smooth logistic and quadratic plug-in classifiers have been extended to the structured setting under the name of maxmargin Markov networks (M<sup>3</sup>N) (Taskar et al., 2004) (or more generally structural SVM (SSVM) (Tsochantaridis et al., 2005))

content.text:
#### 3. Measurability

In [19, 20], Luxemburg and de Pagter related order closed sublattices to measurability in vector lattices. Using their result, we can provide another approach to obtain smallest order closed sublattices. We first recall some definitions from [19]. Let X be an order complete vector lattice with a weak unit u > 0. The set $C_u$ collects all components of u, i.e., all $x \in X$ such that $(u - x) \wedge x = 0$ . A subset $\mathscr{F}$ of $C_u$ is called a complete Boolean subalgebra of $C_u$ if $0 \in \mathscr{F}$ , $u - a \in \mathscr{F}$ for any $a \in \mathscr{F}$ , and $\sup \mathscr{C} \in \mathscr{F}$ for any subset $\mathscr{C}$ of $\mathscr{F}$ . For such $\mathscr{F}$ , a vector $x \in X$ is said to be measurable with respect to $\mathscr{F}$ if $P_{(\lambda u - x)^+}u = \sup_{n \geq 1} (n(\lambda u - x)^+) \wedge u \in \mathscr{F}$ for all $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ . 

For a complete Boolean subalgebra $\mathscr{F}$ of $C_u$ , it is easily seen that $\mathrm{Span}(\mathscr{F})$ is a regular sublattice in X and $\sigma(\mathrm{Span}(\mathscr{F})) = \mathscr{F}$ . Thus, Corollary 3.5 can be viewed as a generalization of [19, Proposition 2.6] which is essentially Freudenthal's Spectral Theorem.

The following is also immediate by Proposition 3.3 and extends [16, Lemma 2.2].

Corollary 3.6. Let X be an order complete vector lattice with a weak unit u > 0, and Y be a sublattice of X containing u. Then Y is order closed if and only if $Y = L_0(\sigma(Y))$ .

**Example 3.7.** Let Y be an order closed sublattice in a Banach function space X over $(\Omega, \Sigma, \mathbb{P})$ . Then there exist $u \in Y_+$ and a $\sigma$ -subalgebra $\mathcal{G}$ of $\Sigma$ such that

$$Y = \{g \in X : g = uh, h \text{ is } \mathcal{G}\text{-}measurable\}.$$

# EXISTENCE AND REGULARITY OF MIN-MAX ANISOTROPIC MINIMAL HYPERSURFACES

GUIDO DE PHILIPPIS, ANTONIO DE ROSA, AND YANGYANG LI

ABSTRACT. In any closed smooth Riemannian manifold of dimension at least three, we use the min-max construction to find anisotropic minimal hypersurfaces with respect to elliptic integrands, with a singular set of codimension 2 vanishing Hausdorff measure. In particular, in a closed 3-manifold, we obtain a smooth anisotropic minimal surface.

The critical step is to obtain a uniform upper bound for density ratios in the anisotropic min-max construction. This confirms a conjecture by Allard [Invent. Math., 1983].

### 1. Introduction

Background and main results. Minimal surfaces are critical points of the area functional. The existence of minimal surfaces in every Riemannian manifold has been a central research theme in Geometric Measure Theory over the past 50 years.

content.title: An interval version of separation by semispaces in max-min convexity
content.text:
# AN INTERVAL VERSION OF SEPARATION BY SEMISPACES IN MAX-MIN CONVEXITY

## VIOREL NITICA AND SERGEĬ SERGEEV

ABSTRACT. In this paper we study separation of a closed box from a max-min convex set by max-min semispaces. This can be regarded as an interval extension of the known separation results. We give a constructive proof of the separation in the case when the box satisfies a certain condition, and we show that the separation is never possible when the condition is not satisfied. We also study the separation of two max-min convex sets by a box and by a box and a semispace. Key Words: fuzzy algebra; tropical convexity; interval; separation; Mathematics Subject Classification 2000: Primary 52A01; Secondary: 52A30, 08A72

## 1. Introduction

Consider the set  $\mathcal{B} = [0,1]$  endowed with the operations  $\oplus = \max, \wedge = \min$ . 

In this paper we study the following interval version of the semispace separation: given a box B, i.e. a Cartesian product of closed intervals, and a max-min convex set C, decide whether it is possible to construct a semispace which contains C and avoids B. In Section 2 we give our main result, Theorem 1, which shows that such separation is indeed possible when B satisfies a certain condition. This condition holds true in particular when B does not contain points with coordinates equal to 1, or when B is reduced to a point. When the condition is not satisfied, we show that the separation by semispaces is never possible. However, separation can be saved if we also allow hemispaces of a certain kind. As a corollary of Theorem 1, we also recover the description of semispaces due to Nitica and Singer [18]. In Section 3 we study the separation of two convex sets by a box and by a box and a semispace.
