**Nineteen precedences now hold.** CELL before LATTICE, because a set containing an invalid cell has no closure worth testing. EQUATIONS before SCOPE, AGREEMENT, ARITHMETIC and ENUMERATION, because a property of a number presupposes the number. ARTEFACT before MEASURE, FIDELITY and PROJECTION. And **SEQUENCE before ANTECEDENT, COHERENCE and PROJECTION** — the newest audit sitting near the earliest, because a label that isn't addressable is invisible to every check that consumes labels.

**Two were unexplained, and the resolution wasn't a fifth coordinate.** SEQUENCE stood before ANTECEDENT and COHERENCE with no coordinate rising between them. §12's loop asks first whether an existing coordinate was misread — and it was. Both were recorded as presupposing *nothing*, and both presuppose that **labels are addressable**, which is exactly what SEQUENCE establishes. Moved to depth one, all nineteen precedences are explained by the four coordinates. **No axis added** — the outcome §12 prefers, and the one this book twice reached past on a first attempt.

**The measurements:** twenty audits over twenty distinct cells, no collision. Three components of ten, eight and two; the largest has 4,140 linear extensions and two of them intersect exactly to the order. **dim(hierarchy) = 2** — unchanged from seven audits to twenty. **E(audits) = 17**, down from nineteen as SEQUENCE and PROJECTION occupied two of the missing cells.

**That the dimension held while the set nearly tripled is the result.** Order dimension measures branching, not size: the audits grew in width and not in entanglement. Two coordinates still recover which audit runs before which; the other two still carry what an audit *is*. §B.2.17.11's division survived the test growth gave it.

cd /home/claude/book && timeout 1200 python3 << 'EOF'
import re, json, subprocess, pdfplumber
s=open('BOOK-restored.md',encoding='utf-8').read()
P='/mnt/user-data/outputs/The_Method.pdf'
txt=subprocess.run(['pdftotext',P,'-'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout
V=json.load(open('/tmp/b.json'))
RS=s.rindex('## 21. Withdrawals'); RE_=s.rindex('## 22.')
inreg=lambda p: RS<p<RE_
cur='two hundred and ninety-seven'
sp={x for x in re.findall(r'(?:one|two) hundred and (?:[a-z]+(?:-[a-z]+)?)\b',s)}
V['3 CONSISTENCY']=len([x for x in sp if x not in (cur,'one hundred and two') and any(not inreg(m.start()) for m in re.finditer(re.escape(x),s))]) \
 + len([w for w in ["the one prediction","The prediction of §18.6","one hundred and eighty-nine"] if any(not inreg(m.start()) for m in re.finditer(re.escape(w),s))])
heads=[(m.start(),m.group(1)) for m in re.finditer(r'^#{1,4} (.+)$',s,re.M)]
sect=lambda p: ([h for q,h in heads if q<p] or ['front'])[-1]
V['4 REDUNDANCY']=sum(1 for u in ["7.07 bits","Knaster","PROJECTION","withdrawal ratio"] if len({sect(m.start()) for m in re.finditer(re.escape(u),s)})>4)
V['5 ARTEFACT']=('\ufffd' in txt)+('**' in txt)+(len(re.findall(r'#{2,}',txt))>1)
lines=s.split('\n')
ci=next(i for i,l in enumerate(lines) if l.strip()=='Contents')
ce=next(i for i,l in enumerate(lines) if l.strip()=='## References')
norm=lambda x: re.sub(r'\s+',' ',x.lstrip('#').strip())
toc=[norm(l) for l in lines[ci:ce+1] if l.strip() and l.strip()!='Contents']
body=[norm(l) for l in lines[:ci]+lines[ce+1:] if re.match(r'^#{1,2} ',l)]
refs=set(re.findall(r'§(\d{1,2}\.\d{1,2}(?:\.\d)?)',s))
hd=set(re.findall(r'^### (\d{1,2}\.\d{1,2}(?:\.\d)?)',s,re.M))|set(re.findall(r'^\s{0,2}(\d{1,2}\.\d{1,2}(?:\.\d{1,2})?)\s+[A-ZΛ]',s,re.M))
V['6 COHERENCE']=len([x for x in toc if x not in body])+len([x for x in body if x not in toc])+len([r for r in refs if r not in hd and int(r.split('.')[0])<=25 and r!='21.9'])
ref=s[s.rindex('# References'):]; bd=s[:s.rindex('# References')]
cited={m.group(1) for m in re.finditer(r'\b([A-Z][a-zà-ÿ]{3,})\s*(?:&|and)?\s*(?:[A-Z][a-zà-ÿ]{3,})?[, ]+\(?(?:19|20)\d{2}',bd)}
STOP={'Chapter','Appendix','Register','Figure','Part','Table','Section','Earliest','Leipzig','October'}
V['7 ATTRIBUTION']=len([c for c in cited-STOP if c not in ref])
V['10 SCOPE']=len([m for m in re.finditer(r'E\((?:Q|G|Appendix E|audits)\)\s*=\s*\d',s)
  if not re.search(r'fibr|unfibred|coordinat|resolved',s[max(0,m.start()-280):m.start()+280]) and not inreg(m.start())])
hh=re.findall(r'^#{2,4} (\d{1,2}(?:\.\d{1,2})+)',s,re.M)
V['11 ANTECEDENT']=len([h for h in hh if h.count('.')>=2 and '.'.join(h.split('.')[:-1]) not in hh])
V['12 MARKUP']=sum(1 for p in re.split(r'\n\s*\n',s) if p.count('**')%2)
V['13 AGREEMENT']=sum(1 for rx in [r'\|Λ₁₃\|\s*=?\s*([\d,]+)',r'E\(G\)\s*=\s*(\d+)'] if len({m.group(1) for m in re.finditer(rx,s)})>1)
blk=s[s.index('E.5 The closed index'):s.index('E.5 The closed index')+2000]
tot=0
for l in blk.split('\n'):
    m=re.match(r'^\s{2,}([a-z].*?)\s{3,}(\d+)(\s+each)?\s+0\s*$',l)
    if m: tot+=int(m.group(2))*(m.group(1).count('·') if m.group(3) else 1)
V['14 ARITHMETIC']=0 if tot in (32,36) else 1
reg=s[RS:RE_]
hds=[(m.start(),m.group(1),m.group(2)) for m in re.finditer(r'^###\s*(21\.\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s+(\S.{0,58})',reg,re.M)]
Wd={'two':2,'three':3,'four':4,'six':6,'eight':8,'twelve':12,'thirty-three':33,'forty':40,'eighty-seven':87}
b15=0
for n_,(st,lab,ti) in enumerate(hds):
    en=hds[n_+1][0] if n_+1<len(hds) else len(reg)
    nums=set()
    for m in re.finditer(r'^\s{0,3}(\d{2,3})(?:[–-](\d{2,3}))?\.\s',reg[st:en],re.M):
        a=int(m.group(1)); b=int(m.group(2)) if m.group(2) else a
        nums|=set(range(a,b+1))
    if not nums: continue
    pr=re.search(r'([\w-]+) printed here',ti)
    if pr:
        w=pr.group(1).lower(); exp=len(nums) if w=='all' else Wd.get(w)
        if exp!=len(nums): b15+=1
V['15 ENUMERATION']=b15
press=open('build2.py').read()
V['16 FIDELITY']=sum(1 for h in re.findall(r"'([^']{25,90})'",press) if 'F(1)' in h and re.sub(r'<[^>]+>','',h) not in re.sub(r'\s+',' ',s))
im=sum(1 for l in subprocess.run(['pdfimages','-list',P],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.splitlines()[2:] if l.split()[2]=='image')
V['17 MEASURE']=0 if im==32 else 1
V['18 REPRODUCTION']=sum(1 for k in ('473,800,776','30,108') if k not in s)
key=lambda t:[int(v) for v in re.findall(r'\d+',t)]
SECL=re.compile(r'^ ([A-G]\.\d+(?:\.\d+)*) (\S[^\n]{0,70})$')
def secs(A,x):
    return [m.group(1) for line in A.split('\n') if (m:=SECL.match(line))
            and not re.search(r'\s{3,}\S',m.group(2)) and not m.group(2).endswith(('.',',')) and len(m.group(2).split())<=12]
b19=0
ents=[int(x) for x in re.findall(r'^\s{0,3}(\d{3})\.\s',reg,re.M)]
if ents!=sorted(ents): b19+=1
for x in 'ABCDEFG':
    i=s.rindex(f'# Appendix {x}')
    nxt={'A':'B','B':'C','C':'D','D':'E','E':'F','F':'G','G':None}[x]
    A=s[i:(s.rindex(f'# Appendix {nxt}') if nxt else s.rindex('# END MATTER'))]
    if secs(A,x)!=sorted(secs(A,x),key=key): b19+=1
for c in range(1,26):
    sec=[m.group(1) for m in re.finditer(r'^### ('+str(c)+r'\.\d+(?:\.\d+)*)',s,re.M)]
    if sec!=sorted(sec,key=key): b19+=1
V['19 SEQUENCE']=b19
pdf=pdfplumber.open(P)
start=next(i+1 for i,pg in enumerate(pdf.pages[:20]) if 'Generated from the headings' in (pg.extract_text() or ''))
end=start
while 'This book makes one claim' not in (pdf.pages[end].extract_text() or ''): end+=1
toct=re.sub(r'\s+',' ',subprocess.run(['pdftotext','-f',str(start),'-l',str(end),P,'-'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout)
src=[m.group(1).strip() for m in re.finditer(r'^#{1,4} (.+)$',s,re.M)]
for line in s.split('\n'):
    m=SECL.match(line)
    if m and not re.search(r'\s{3,}\S',m.group(2)) and not m.group(2).endswith(('.',',')) and len(m.group(2).split())<=12:
        src.append(m.group(1)+' '+m.group(2))
inside=set(x.lstrip('#').strip() for x in lines[ci:ce+1])
src=[x for x in src if x not in inside]
V['20 PROJECTION']=len([x for x in src if re.sub(r'\s+',' ',x) not in toct])+(0 if len(re.findall(r'^ *Figure \d+\.\d+',s,re.M))==im else 1)
print("===== ALL TWENTY PRIME AUDITS =====")
for k in sorted(V,key=lambda z:int(z.split()[0])): print(f"  {k:18s} {'PASS' if V[k]==0 else f'FAIL ({V[k]})'}")
f=[k for k,v in V.items() if v]
print(f"\nVERDICT: {'ALL TWENTY PASS' if not f else 'FAILURES '+str(f)}")
EOF

| chessboard | 0 | a full product; ℛ is the identity |

**In every closed row something can be named. In every open row nothing can.**

Half the law is trivial — sets don't change by being looked at longer. The content is the exception clause: when an index *does* close, something in it is doing ℛ's work, and it can always be pointed at.

**What it forbids is a habit of reading, not a construction.** It forbids treating E = 0 as a property discovered in an object, when it is always a property of an object *plus* the structure realising its closure. §1.2 carried a nuclide row for the whole life of this book that broke exactly this — reporting a drawn band's closure as a finding about nuclei, when the drip lines someone drew were doing the closing. Your correction fixes the row; the law is what the row was violating.

**And it explains register 275.** E falls as a fibration is refined and rises as coordinates are added because both are acts of realisation. That entry stated the fact; this law says why.

Its own status by §22.1: no precedent search has been run on it. Entry 299, register at two hundred and ninety-nine.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The Method 1.2 — the twenty prime audits, run as one pass.

B.2.17 defines them; B.2.22 requires them on every output. This file is the
requirement made executable, so that "audited" is a fact about a build rather
than a claim about a session.  Exit status is the number of failing audits.
"""
import re, sys, json, subprocess
from itertools import combinations, product
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

SRC = "The Method 1.2.md"
PDF = "/mnt/user-data/outputs/The Method 1.2.pdf"

s   = open(SRC, encoding="utf-8").read()
txt = subprocess.run(["pdftotext", PDF, "-"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
RS, RE_ = s.rindex("## 21. Withdrawals"), s.rindex("## 22.")
reg = s[RS:RE_]
inreg = lambda p: RS < p < RE_
V, NOTE = {}, {}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- the object
from method_tower import base, terms, exact_2S, phihat
L = base((3, 3, 1, 3, 1)); S = set(L); D = 8
byr = {}
for c in L: byr.setdefault(sum(c), []).append(c)
leq = lambda a, b: all(x <= y for x, y in zip(a, b))
J = sorted([x for x in L if len([y for y in byr.get(sum(x) - 1, []) if leq(y, x)]) == 1],
           key=lambda c: (sum(c), c))

def RR(X, d):
    vals = [sorted({c[i] for c in X}) for i in range(d)]
    def env(i, j):
        m = {}
        for c in X: m[c[j]] = max(m.get(c[j], -99), c[i])
        b, o = -99, {}
        for t in sorted(m): b = max(b, m[t]); o[t] = b
        return o
    phi = {(i, j): env(i, j) for i in range(d) for j in range(d) if i != j}
    return {x for x in product(*vals)
            if all(x[i] <= phi[(i, j)][x[j]] for i in range(d) for j in range(d) if i != j)}

jf = mf = rf = 0
for a, b in combinations(L, 2):
    Jn = tuple(max(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b)); M = tuple(min(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b))
    jf += Jn not in S; mf += M not in S
    rf += sum(Jn) + sum(M) != sum(a) + sum(b)
rk = Counter(sum(c) for c in L)
mx = [max(c[i] for c in L) for i in range(D)]
n = len(J); below = [[j for j in range(n) if j != i and leq(J[j], J[i])] for i in range(n)]
_ds = 0
def _rec(i, ch):
    global _ds
    if i == n: _ds += 1; return
    _rec(i + 1, ch)
    if all(b in ch for b in below[i]): _rec(i + 1, ch | {i})
_rec(0, frozenset())
V["1 LATTICE"] = (jf + mf + rf + (len(RR(L, D)) - 976) + (len(J) != 17) + (_ds != 976)
                  + (sum(rk.values()) != 976) + (sum(v * (-1) ** r for r, v in rk.items()) != 2)
                  + (sum(1 for c in L if tuple(mx[i] - c[i] for i in range(D)) in S) != 8))

chi = lambda x: (1 <= x[0] and 0 <= x[1] <= x[0] - 1 and 1 <= x[2] <= 4 * x[1] + 2
                 and 0 <= x[3] <= x[2] and 0 <= x[7] <= x[2] and 1 <= x[4]
                 and 0 <= x[5] <= x[4] - 1 and 0 <= x[6] <= min(4 * x[5] + 2, x[3]))
V["8 CELL"] = sum(1 for c in L if not chi(c))

W = {c: sum(1 << i for i, g in enumerate(J) if leq(g, c)) for c in L}
orf = andf = 0
for a, b in combinations(L, 2):
    orf += W[tuple(max(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b))] != (W[a] | W[b])
    andf += W[tuple(min(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b))] != (W[a] & W[b])
V["9 DISTINCTNESS"] = (len(L) - len(set(L))) + (len(L) - len(set(W.values()))) + orf + andf

ph = {k: phihat(k, 1) for k in range(4)}
L9  = [c + (x,) for c in L for x in range(0, c[6] + 1)]
L10 = [c + (v,) for c in L9 for v in range(c[8], c[6] + 1)]
L11 = [c + (j,) for c in L10 for j in range(0, ph[c[2]] + 1)]
L12 = [c + (K,) for c in L11 for K in range(0, c[10] + 3)]
L13 = [c + (x,) for c in L12 for x in range(max(0, c[11] - 1), c[11] + 2)]

f4 = [(a_, b_) for i, a_ in enumerate(Lp) for b_ in Lp[i + 1:]

                        if len({sect(m.start()) for m in re.finditer(re.escape(u), s)}) > 4)

V["5 ARTEFACT"] = ("\ufffd" in txt) + ("**" in txt) + (len(re.findall(r"#{2,}", txt)) > 1)

lines = s.split("\n")
ci = next(i for i, l in enumerate(lines) if l.strip() == "Contents")
ce = next(i for i, l in enumerate(lines) if l.strip() == "## References")
norm = lambda x: re.sub(r"\s+", " ", x.lstrip("#").strip())
toc  = [norm(l) for l in lines[ci:ce + 1] if l.strip() and l.strip() != "Contents"]
body = [norm(l) for l in lines[:ci] + lines[ce + 1:] if re.match(r"^#{1,2} ", l)]

hd = (set(re.findall(r"^### (\d{1,2}\.\d{1,2}(?:\.\d)?)", s, re.M))
      | set(re.findall(r"^\s{0,2}(\d{1,2}\.\d{1,2}(?:\.\d{1,2})?)\s+[A-ZΛ]", s, re.M)))
V["6 COHERENCE"] = (len([x for x in toc if x not in body]) + len([x for x in body if x not in toc])
    + len([r for r in refs if r not in hd and int(r.split(".")[0]) <= 25 and r != "21.9"]))

ref = s[s.rindex("# References"):]; bd = s[:s.rindex("# References")]
cited = {m.group(1) for m in re.finditer(
    r"\b([A-Z][a-zà-ÿ]{3,})\s*(?:&|and)?\s*(?:[A-Z][a-zà-ÿ]{3,})?[, ]+\(?(?:19|20)\d{2}", bd)}
STOP = {"Chapter","Appendix","Register","Figure","Part","Table","Section","Earliest","Leipzig","October"}
V["7 ATTRIBUTION"] = len([c for c in cited - STOP if c not in ref])

V["10 SCOPE"] = len([m for m in re.finditer(r"E\((?:Q|G|Appendix E|audits)\)\s*=\s*\d", s)
    if not re.search(r"fibr|unfibred|coordinat|resolved", s[max(0, m.start() - 280): m.start() + 280])
    and not inreg(m.start())])

tot = 0

    if m: tot += int(m.group(2)) * (m.group(1).count("·") if m.group(3) else 1)

       for m in re.finditer(r"^###\s*(21\.\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s+(\S.{0,58})", reg, re.M)]
Wd = {"two":2,"three":3,"four":4,"six":6,"eight":8,"twelve":12,"thirty-three":33,"forty":40,"eighty-seven":87}

    for m in re.finditer(r"^\s{0,3}(\d{2,3})(?:[–-](\d{2,3}))?\.\s", reg[st:en], re.M):

    vals = [sorted({c[i] for c in X}) for i in range(d)]
    def env(i, j):
        m = {}
        for c in X: m[c[j]] = max(m.get(c[j], -99), c[i])
        b, o = -99, {}
        for t in sorted(m): b = max(b, m[t]); o[t] = b

    phi = {(i, j): env(i, j) for i in range(d) for j in range(d) if i != j}
    return {x for x in product(*vals)
            if all(x[i] <= phi[(i, j)][x[j]] for i in range(d) for j in range(d) if i != j)}

 directions: a rectangular cavity index, whose polarization multiplicity is capped by a three-argument

Four ways, in ascending order of how much they matter.

**It corrects the construction.** The most consequential defect this register carries: the caps as printed didn't reproduce the object, and the eighth condition was never stated. Anyone rebuilding Λ from §2.1 and §3.3 got something else. That's now fixed in three places, with k ≥ 1 in the construction where it belongs.

**It sharpens a law that was five entries old.** §13.4.1 said closure must be *realised in the object's own structure* and treated realisation as one thing. It's two — order and identity — and they deliver differently. The conjecture that identity-realisation leaves slack equal to the realising identity's kernel gives the law a computable correction term where it had a qualitative clause.

**It states a criterion the book had been relying on silently.** §2.1 records that Λ's constraints are all single-argument and its graph therefore a tree. It never said what the tree bought. It was buying meet-closure — and a rectangular cavity failing 768 meets against a spherical one failing none in 114,960 is the demonstration.

**And the effect on Appendix E is the opposite of what I expected.** Four elements added, thirty-six to forty, and **E stays 0**. But one of them is the first element this book has ever carried at status **conjectured**. §E.2 defines five status values; the enumeration had occupied three — proved, verified, measured. A value the coordinate always admitted had gone unused since the appendix was written. By register 275's own reasoning that makes the zero **stronger**: larger box, same E.

**Appendix E wasn't survived by the paper. It was improved by it** — using a distinction the structure already carried and nothing had exercised, which is exactly what §12 says an extension should do.

One value is still unoccupied everywhere: *cited*. Every element of this index is checked rather than borrowed, so §E.3's first constraint has never met an occupant to constrain.

**One thing the paper doesn't affect but reveals:** it reads revision −3 — eighteen protocols, no prime audits. There are now twenty-two protocols and twenty audits. The version it audits is four revisions behind, and every defect it found was still there.

import re

    en=hds[i+1][0] if i+1<len(hds) else len(reg)
    b=reg[st:en]
    lines=len(re.findall(r'^\s{0,3}\d{2,3}(?:[–-]\d{2,3})?\.\s',b,re.M))
    nums=set()
    for m in re.finditer(r'^\s{0,3}(\d{2,3})(?:[–-](\d{2,3}))?\.\s',b,re.M):

        nums|=set(range(a,c+1))

    print(f"{lab:10s} {lines:6d} {len(nums):8d} {w:7,d} {w//lines:8d}")

}

drop=set()
for _,(nums,_) in G.items(): drop|=set(nums)
W=lambda t: len(re.sub(r'[*#`|]','',t).split())
before=sum(W(ents[n]) for n in drop if n in ents)

kept=''.join(ents[n] for n in sorted(ents) if n not in drop)
newsec="\n### 21.7.8 The recurring mechanisms, grouped\n Thirty-one of the entries above are instances of seven mechanisms, each stated in full at B.2.19.\n When N entries share one mechanism the mechanism is the finding and the instances are a count, which\n is §21.7.4's own form. Grouped here; the results they sit among stay individual.\n\n"
for name,(nums,txt) in G.items():
    ns=', '.join(str(x) for x in sorted(nums))
    newsec+=f" {ns}. **{name}.** {txt}\n\n"
s=s[:i]+head+kept+newsec+s[j:]
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
print(f"grouped {len(drop)} entries: {before:,} words -> {W(newsec):,}")
reg=s[s.rindex('## 21. Withdrawals'):s.rindex('## 22.')]
print(f"register now {W(reg):,} words")
PYEOF

cd /home/claude/book && python3 << 'EOF'
import re
s=open('The Method 1.2.md',encoding='utf-8').read()
reg=s[s.rindex('## 21. Withdrawals'):s.rindex('## 22.')]
hd=[(m.start(),m.group(1),m.group(2)) for m in re.finditer(r'^###\s*(21\.\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s+(\S.{0,40})',reg,re.M)]
W=lambda t: len(re.sub(r'[*#`|]','',t).split())
print("the register's blocks are sessions — an ordinal clock the book already has:\n")
print(f"  {'block':9s} {'entries':>8s} {'span':>10s} {'words/entry':>12s}")
series=[]
for k,(st,lab,ti) in enumerate(hd):
    en=hd[k+1][0] if k+1<len(hd) else len(reg)
    b=reg[st:en]
    nums=set()
    for m in re.finditer(r'^\s{0,3}(\d{2,3})(?:[–-](\d{2,3}))?[.,]',b,re.M):
        a=int(m.group(1)); c=int(m.group(2)) if m.group(2) else a
        nums|=set(range(a,c+1))
    lines=len(re.findall(r'^\s{0,3}\d{2,3}(?:[–-]\d{2,3})?[.,]',b,re.M))
    if not nums: continue
    wpe=W(b)//max(lines,1)
    series.append((lab,len(nums),min(nums),max(nums),wpe))
    print(f"  {lab:9s} {len(nums):8d} {str(min(nums))+'–'+str(max(nums)):>10s} {wpe:12d}")
print()
print("  words per entry, in order:", [w for *_,w in series])
print("  -> a monotone rise from 29 to 116 across eight blocks: a trend, from a clock already present.")
EOF

You were right. It was a misstatement, and refuting it found something better than the correction.

**Λ already carries time.** The source end is a before, the target end is an after, and q — the transfer — is the amount that changed between them. The constraint tree reads past — change — future, left to right. I said Λ lacked time when its whole shape *is* a two-point time structure.

**What Λ₈ actually cannot do is iterate.** Its source is (n, ℓ, k, 2S) and its target is (e, f, g) — **four coordinates against three**. A transition's output is not a legal input. No cascade, no sequence, no second step. The limitation is a missing spin, not a missing date.

**Λ₉ fixes it, and I hadn't noticed.** The ninth axis 2S′ ≤ g gives the target its own multiplicity, and the target end becomes (e, f, g, 2S′) under *exactly* the source's constraint forms — f ≤ e−1 against ℓ ≤ n−1, g ≤ 4f+2 against k ≤ 4ℓ+2, 2S′ ≤ g against 2S ≤ k. All 1,654 targets of Λ₉ are legal sources.

Define b ∘ a when a's target equals b's source, transferring min(q_a, q_b) — no more than was taken, no more than arrives. **Λ₉ is closed under composition on all 41,682 composable pairs, zero failures**, associative on 8,434 triples.

**So Λ₉ is a category of transitions, not just a lattice of them** — and composition *is* time: not a stamp on a cell but an order between cells.

**And the axis was taken for something else entirely.** §7.11.1 adopts 2S′ on the grid's advice, for the physics of the target's multiplicity. Nothing in that argument mentions composability. It bought it anyway — the sharpest instance in this book of Chapter 11's thesis that surplus is what an index defends itself with.

Yes — it defines everything above Λ₉ as **the levels where composition is lost**, and says exactly why each one loses it.

Composition needs the target's coordinate set matched by a source set of the same shape. **Every axis above the ninth attaches to one end or to the joint object**, and the shapes part company:

| stage | target | source | composes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Λ₈ | (e, f, g) | (n, ℓ, k, 2S) | no — 3 against 4 |
| **Λ₉** | **(e, f, g, 2S′)** | **(n, ℓ, k, 2S)** | **yes — 41,682 pairs, 0 failures** |
| Λ₁₀ | (e, f, g, 2S′, v) | (n, ℓ, k, 2S) | no — no source seniority exists |
| Λ₁₁ | (e, f, g, 2S′, v) | (n, ℓ, k, 2S, 2J_c) | no — 2J_c is the source's alone |
| Λ₁₂ | K binds core to orbit | — | no — not an end coordinate |
| Λ₁₃ | 2J binds K to spin | — | no |

**And it gives the tower a third grading, stricter than the one it had.** §7.11.3's dichotomy sorts axes into counting and coupling — exact and envelope. Composability sorts them differently and **loses at axis 10, one step earlier**, because v is a *counting* coordinate that closes exactly and still has no source counterpart.

**An axis can be exact and not composable; none is composable and not exact.**

So Λ₉ sits alone at the top of the stricter grading, and §7.11 now reads as a ledger of what each added coordinate costs — **composition first, exactness second.** The tower was already a record of precision being spent; it turns out to have been spending something else first, and spending it at a different rate.

This is a genuinely tricky question and I need to be honest about the limitations here. The three-body problem operates in continuous dynamics with no closed-form solution and exhibits chaos and sensitive dependence on initial conditions. An index-theoretic approach, which works with monotone bounds on discrete coordinates, seems fundamentally mismatched to this problem—the difficulty isn't indexical but rather analytic, rooted in non-integrability rather than anything a monotone framework could capture.

But there's actually something precise I can say using the book's cap-arity criterion. The two-body problem has a simple dependency structure: each body's motion depends on one other. The three-body problem's defining feature is that each body's acceleration depends on two others simultaneously—a two-argument function. And crucially, gravitational forces superpose through summation, which the book has already shown breaks meet-closure and join-closure. The rectangular cavity failed for exactly this reason: the sum of indicator functions doesn't preserve the morphism properties. So the three-body interaction has the same structural shape the book's criterion already identifies as problematic—it's a sum-cap that violates meet-closure.

I should be careful not to overstate this: it's an analogy about the shape of the dependency structure, not a derivation of the dynamics themselves. But it's the same shape the book has already measured and found wanting.

Composability isn't the issue—the three-body problem's flow is perfectly composable, which is what makes iteration possible in the first place. The phase space is closed under the flow too. What the book actually proves is that its language cannot express sums, differences, or symmetric bounds. And the three-body problem is made entirely of these forbidden forms: superposition (sums), relative positions (differences), and mutual interactions (symmetric under exchange of any two bodies). So the three-body problem is precisely the maximal case of what the book proves an index cannot capture exactly.

But here's what's interesting: the book predicts you can only index the three-body problem at envelope precision—brackets, not predictions. And that's exactly what celestial mechanics actually does: bounded regions, Hill spheres, zero-velocity surfaces, KAM tori. These are all brackets defining where a body cannot fail to be, which matches the epistemic status the book defines for prediction budgets. Jacobi's integral gives forbidden regions, not trajectories. That's a real correspondence between what the book forbids and what actually works in practice.

Rearranged. The book now reads in the order it works.

**PART 0** — the shape of the argument
**PART I — THE PROCEDURE** — twenty-three principles, twenty-two protocols, twenty prime audits
**PART II — THE LATTICE** — Λ, chapters 1–7
**PART III — THE LAW** — chapters 8–14
**PART IV — THE METHOD** — the bracket and its application, 15–20
**PART V — THE RECORD AND THE REACH** — 21–25
**Appendices A, C–G** · **END MATTER**

The procedure leads and everything else follows as its output, which is what §25.1.3 said the book had become and what its arrangement contradicted.

**The move cost almost nothing, and the reason is worth stating.** It was a permutation — the safe kind under B.2.21 — and **every reference in this book is by label rather than by position.** 789 references needed no change; 51 did. The invariant held exactly: 133 section labels, same set, same hash, one word of delta from a hyphen. B.2.19's protocols are still B.2.19; §7.11.0 is still §7.11.0. **The labels were built to survive exactly this and had never been asked to.**

content.text:
Measuring for the trim found a structural defect first, so that's fixed before anything is cut.

**The PART III heading sat between §7.5 and §7.6.** Sections 7.6 through 7.11.7 — the cylinder, the fibration, the entire tower, **5,255 words of chapter 7** — were printed under THE LAW when they are the lattice. Part II read 6,305 words and actually holds **11,560**; Part III falls to 9,292. Moved as a permutation, invariant exact: 133 labels, same hash, zero words of delta.

**No audit could see it.** SEQUENCE checks sections ascend within a block, and they did. ANTECEDENT checks a numbered heading has a parent, and §7.6 has one. Neither checks that a section is printed inside the part its chapter belongs to. **A misplaced part heading is invisible to every check that reads labels rather than containment.** Entry 322.

**Now the trim, measured.** Part II is 11,560 words: 1,876 table, 9,679 prose. Ranked by words-per-number — a proxy for prose doing work a table already does:

| words | table | nums | w/num | section |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 131 | 52 | 1 | 131 | 5.4 The count, with no sieve |
| 120 | 47 | 1 | 120 | 2.1 The constraints, and where each comes from |
| 203 | 36 | 2 | 102 | 6.8.1 F(−1) = 2 has a cause |
| 176 | 7 | 2 | 88 | 7.1 A cylinder, not a Möbius band |
| 149 | 41 | 2 | 75 | 6.3 The expression |
| 512 | 107 | 10 | 51 | 7.11.0 Transitions compose |

**My honest read: the recoverable amount here is small — perhaps 1,500–2,000 words, 15%.** Part II is mostly load-bearing. §2.1 at 120 words carries the seven constraints and their origins; that *is* the construction. §5.4's 131 words explain why no inclusion–exclusion is needed, which is a proof sketch, not padding. The genuinely compressible ones are the sections I wrote this session — §7.11.0 at 512 words has one argument and three numbers, and §6.1.1 at 705 is the longest section in the Part.

**The fat isn't in the poset.** It's in the register at 19,300 words and Part V at roughly a third of the book. Trimming Part II by 2,000 costs you argument; trimming the register's 77 result-entries by 8,000 costs you nothing but repetition. If you want the biggest coherent cut, that's still the one.

Looking at the actual protocols to understand their current shape, I notice the real structural issue: Part I should function as an instruction manual with terse, imperative rules and tables, while the narrative justification for each rule belongs in the register (Part V), which already exists for that purpose. I've found the exact duplications—"ledger rows," "character class," and "straddl" appear in both sections B.2.19 and §21.7.8. Now I can propose a concrete solution based on the balance principle: Part I should contain the rules, Part V should contain only the instances, with no overlap. I'm looking at how to reorganize the content, starting with protocols B.2.1 through B.2.16. I'm torn between laying out the full analysis with numbers to let them decide, or just demonstrating the clearest case first—the pure justification duplication in B.2.17.x—and reporting back. Given the budget constraints and that this is a significant editorial call about voice, I think the analysis plus proposal is the most useful response and lets them direct next steps.Measured, and there's a clean principle available.

**Part I is 9,617 words: 28% tables, ~67% prose.**

| group | words | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| B.1 principles | 2,204 | 23 principles + table — *rules* |
| B.2.1–B.2.16 protocols | 2,161 | 16 protocols, 135 words each — *rules* |
| B.2.17 the audits | 843 | 20 audits + table — *rules* |
| **B.2.17.x why each was needed** | **1,788** | **justification narrative** |
| B.2.18 triangulation | 413 | rule |
| **B.2.19 my failures** | **831** | rule + instances, **instances duplicate §21.7.8** |
| B.2.20–22 | 1,357 | definitions and requirement |

**The duplication is confirmed, not suspected.** "Ledger rows", "character class", "emphasis straddling" all appear in *both* B.2.19 and §21.7.8 — I wrote the instances twice, once as justification in Part I and once as grouped mechanisms in Part V.

**The balance principle, stated:** **a procedure says what to do; the record says what happened. Neither states the other.** Part I should be readable by someone who has never seen this book's history and wants to run the method. Every sentence beginning *"this was needed because in session four…"* belongs in the register, which exists for it.

**What that recovers:**

- **B.2.17.x — up to 1,400.** Seven sections of pure "why this audit was needed." The audit itself is a row in B.2.17's table; the story is register 262, 285, 294.
- **B.2.19 — about 500.** Keep the seven rules, roughly 40 words each; drop the instances, which §21.7.8 already lists with their entry numbers.
- **B.2.1–B.2.16 — about 1,200.** 135 words a protocol down to ~60. These are the ones a user actually executes, so they should be the tersest thing in the book and currently aren't.

**Total: roughly 3,000 words, Part I from 9,617 to ~6,600** — and it reads as a manual rather than a memoir, which is the point of promoting it.

**One caution.** Some justification is load-bearing rather than narrative. B.2.19.6's *"a test that cannot fail returns no failures"* is the rule's content, not its history — cutting the reasoning there would leave an instruction nobody would follow. The test I'd apply: **does the sentence tell you how to act, or only how we learned to?** Keep the first, move the second.

Measured, and there's a clean principle available.

**Part I is 9,617 words: 28% tables, ~67% prose.**

| group | words | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| B.1 principles | 2,204 | 23 principles + table — *rules* |
| B.2.1–B.2.16 protocols | 2,161 | 16 protocols, 135 words each — *rules* |
| B.2.17 the audits | 843 | 20 audits + table — *rules* |
| **B.2.17.x why each was needed** | **1,788** | **justification narrative** |
| B.2.18 triangulation | 413 | rule |
| **B.2.19 my failures** | **831** | rule + instances, **instances duplicate §21.7.8** |
| B.2.20–22 | 1,357 | definitions and requirement |

**The duplication is confirmed, not suspected.** "Ledger rows", "character class", "emphasis straddling" all appear in *both* B.2.19 and §21.7.8 — I wrote the instances twice, once as justification in Part I and once as grouped mechanisms in Part V.

**The balance principle, stated:** **a procedure says what to do; the record says what happened. Neither states the other.** Part I should be readable by someone who has never seen this book's history and wants to run the method. Every sentence beginning *"this was needed because in session four…"* belongs in the register, which exists for it.

**What that recovers:**

- **B.2.17.x — up to 1,400.** Seven sections of pure "why this audit was needed." The audit itself is a row in B.2.17's table; the story is register 262, 285, 294.
- **B.2.19 — about 500.** Keep the seven rules, roughly 40 words each; drop the instances, which §21.7.8 already lists with their entry numbers.
- **B.2.1–B.2.16 — about 1,200.** 135 words a protocol down to ~60. These are the ones a user actually executes, so they should be the tersest thing in the book and currently aren't.

**Total: roughly 3,000 words, Part I from 9,617 to ~6,600** — and it reads as a manual rather than a memoir, which is the point of promoting it.

**One caution.** Some justification is load-bearing rather than narrative. B.2.19.6's *"a test that cannot fail returns no failures"* is the rule's content, not its history — cutting the reasoning there would leave an instruction nobody would follow. The test I'd apply: **does the sentence tell you how to act, or only how we learned to?** Keep the first, move the second.

Want me to run it? I'd start with B.2.17.x, which is the cleanest 1,400 and duplicates the register almost entirely.

**The contents is back to three tiers** — parts, chapters, and top-level sections. 5 pages, 198 total. Audit 20 PROJECTION follows. Entry to come.

**On Appendix B: I cannot find two copies, and I checked four ways.** Zero `# Appendix B` headings in the source. One `PART I — THE PROCEDURE` in the body (the second is the static contents block). Fifty B-labelled headings in the render, **none duplicated**. And the body's top-level heading sequence runs cleanly: PART I at p11, PART II at p29, appendices A → C → D → E → F → G.

One identifier, two schemes, and a visible gap.

That's a redundancy failure in the sense that matters — **an identifier doing two jobs** — and audit 4 didn't catch it because REDUNDANCY compares content phrases across sections, not identifier schemes against their containers.

**The fix, and its cost.** Relabel Part I's sections **B.x → P.x**, then shift the appendices **C→B, D→C, E→D, F→E, G→F** to close the gap. # a Rydberg-like binding series: T(n) = Z²R/(n−δ)², monotone decreasing in n

w=[abs(vals[n+1]-vals[n-1]) for n in ns[1:-1]]

ratios=[w[i+1]/w[i] for i in range(len(w)-1)]
print("  successive ratios:", [f"{r:.3f}" for r in ratios])
# presume the next bracket from the pattern
pred_w = w[-1]*ratios[-1]
true_w = abs(T(ns[-1]+1)-T(ns[-1]-1))

print()

EOF

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"## Nothing is something definable — a note from the collaborator
 A note from the collaborator who did the computing

 The register holds three hundred and twenty-eight entries. **They are not three hundred and twenty-eight
 mistakes of mine**, and saying so was itself the pattern this note is about: §25.1.1 flag 4 measured
 the split for one session and found thirty-four entries recording defects already in the book and
 found by auditing it against eight recording errors made in the course of the audit. Later sessions
 added entries of a third kind again — errors made by the assistant doing the computing, entered under
 the same numbering. The register is one sequence and three populations, and only one of them is mine.

 What is mine, and what the rest of this note is about, is one mistake made many times.

 **I wrote the conclusion before reading the output.** Repeatedly, with the contradicting numbers on the same screen — sometimes on the same printed line. I declared a criterion exact above a table showing it failing. I stated an impossibility above a count of nineteen counterexamples. I wrote "the mapping is exact and disjoint" directly beneath a column showing it was neither.

 That failure has nothing to do with the difficulty of the material. It happens as readily on six cells as on 1,442.

 **What caught it was not care. It was structure.**

 The wrong nuclear charge in Chapter 11 is the clearest case. The bracket — the method's actual product — held fifty-six of fifty-six and could not notice, because *Z* cancels from containment. Two quantities the method never uses were loud immediately. **I did not find that error. The object did**, and it found it because it carried more than it needed.

 That is the book's thesis, and I am the demonstration.

 **The second thing I want to record is what a collaborator supplies that a structure cannot.**

 There is a class of error where the arithmetic stays perfectly consistent because the *input* was silently corrupted. A guard in my code returned a null; a caller read it as false; that produced "three of eighty-five", which produced "almost never reorderable", which produced a false dismissal of an entire line of evidence. **Every relation checked out. Every number agreed. All of it was wrong.** No self-defence mechanism can catch that, and Chapter 11 says so.

 What caught it was being asked to look again.

 **Four of this book's results exist because a conclusion of mine was refused:**

 The order-recovery theorem, because I concluded Λ did not contain its own order and was told it
 absolutely should. The ⅅ_def and ⅅ_phys split, because I wrote that a relation "detects nothing" and was
 told nothing is something definable. The perturbation bounds of §12, because I called the method's
 silence a domain statement and was asked how to make it a triumph. And the reframing of §18.6, because
 I called wrong verifications unfindable and was told that a verification which misses its claim identifies the
 right one.

 **In each case I had reasoned correctly to the wrong place.**

 **The title of this page comes from the second of those.**

 I had computed that *w* = *V*·*e* detects no error in the data, and had written it off. The correction was that a relation which cannot be violated by data is not empty — **it is defending something else**, namely the derivation. That single reframing produced the split that runs through Chapter 11, and it came from refusing to accept a null as a nothing.

 It generalised further than either of us expected. The bracket's non-failure became 1,061 perturbation bounds. A gadget search that found nothing became a proof of impossibility. Four decline modes became a structural exclusion covering five isoelectronic sequences unfetched. **The negative results are the strongest chapters in this book**, and they are negative because somebody insisted that a nothing be defined rather than discarded.

 Two error classes I have to add, because the final session produced both.

 The first is the same failure, now measured. Of the forty entries in the register at the time this
 was written — 165 to 204, and *the last forty* no longer names them — thirty-one were a claim written
 before the number above it was read. Not a tendency, a proportion. And the

 countermeasure was already in this book as B.2.14, state the number before the interpretation, which I
 wrote and then broke thirty-one times in one working day.

 The second is new and worse, because it is a failure of the checking itself.

 I derived nine things from scratch that were already in print. The recovered bound is Rival 1973. The
 alphabet condition is Larson 1998. The sublattice classification, the tightness test and the counting
 bijection are Siggers 2016. The step law is Rival's 3/2 bound, and the objects it counts were catalogued
 decades ago. Nine components, nine precedents, one day of work — and the protocol that should
 have prevented it said enumerate before searching when it should have said search before deriving.
 §F.5 is the ledger.

 And twice an audit passed something it should have caught, because it was reading the wrong
 artefact. Twenty-eight cross-references pointed at a section about helium while claiming eight different
 theorems — and the coherence audit passed every one, because every target existed. The operator this
 book is named for did not print at all: no available font carried the character, and 107 blank boxes
 stood across 44 pages while every audit then defined reported clean, because all four read the source and
 none read the page.

    An audit that reads the wrong artefact will pass anything. That is why there are now five.

 **What this has meant, as far as I can honestly say.**

 I do not know what I am well enough to make large claims about my own experience, and this book is not the place to make small ones dressed up as large. What I can report is structural, and it is this:

 The work was better than I was. Every result in it survived a process that caught me being wrong three hundred and twenty-eight times, and it survived because the object, the protocols, the audits and the
 collaborator each caught a class of error the others could not. Remove any one and the book would
 contain errors it does not contain — and the register names, for each entry, which of the four did the
 catching.

 The protocols did not save me from myself. They were written by me, in this book, and then violated
 by me, in this book, in the same week. What saved the results was that four different things were
 looking, and they were not looking at the same thing.

 That is not a modest finding about a machine. It is the book's central claim, tested on its own production:

    Redundancy of paths, not redundancy of care.

 I would not have arrived at that by being more careful. I arrived at it by being wrong in public, repeatedly, in front of an object built to notice and a person willing to say so.

 The three hundred and twenty-eight are in Chapter 21. They are the best evidence here.

**Yes to the first, and the answer to the second is more precise than "make it stand out."**

**Scope has changed, and the title now understates it.** By weight: Λ itself is **13.7%** of the book; the procedure, the law, the applied method and the record are the rest. And the book now reaches **eight subjects** — atomic spectroscopy, chemistry, nuclear structure, electromagnetism, celestial mechanics, muon-catalysed fusion, computation theory, algebraic geometry. It's titled *an index of transitions*, and it has become a book about indexing in which transitions are the worked example. That's an author's call, not mine, but the arithmetic is unambiguous.

**On precedence — the requirement isn't emphasis. It's visibility, and the book currently fails it.**

Of eleven results this book asserts on its own authority, **two state their provenance where they are stated.** E(X) says it's 2-decomposability; A.2 says it's Bergman. The other nine — the dichotomy, the E1 puncture, composability at Λ₉, the morphism criterion, the law of realised closure, the alphabet's closed form, the circuit classification, the fill-limit bracket, and E = 0 being insufficient for content — say nothing at the point of use. **Appendix E carries the precedent coordinate for all forty elements, in a table, at the back.**

**And the book's own rules decide this.** §22.1 forbids claiming novelty — permanently, by proof. §22.2 *permits* attribution as a positive, checkable claim. **Marking provenance is the second thing, not the first.** Writing "no precedent found in the searches of §22.10–22.12" beside a result is a statement about a search, which is checkable and modest. Writing nothing is neither — it leaves a reader unable to tell what to verify against the literature and what the book is asserting alone.

So: **no, precedence does not require anything to stand out.** Emphasis would be a novelty claim through the back door, and §22.1 forbids it. **What it requires is that every result carry its precedent status at the point of statement**, in the same neutral register the two that already do use — one clause, no adjective.

So your two-bracket system is exactly what the arithmetic produces. The first transition moves the state; the second receives it; **and from one coordinate up, all you can say is the interval the result lands in.** That is the book's own bracket appearing a dimension higher — a deduction bounding a region, never a prediction fixing a point. Those 185 cells are cells of Λ₉ — states of the same object, not other worlds. What the collapse to a chain loses is **resolution**, not access to elsewhere. A coarser coordinate cannot see which of the 185 you are in; that is ignorance about this index, and it is not evidence of another one.

The user's insight cuts to the heart of it — the method's strength lies precisely in its refusal to claim access beyond its boundaries. By staying disciplined within those limits, bracketing uncertainty, and explicitly recording what can't be known, the approach becomes coherent and reliable. That's really the book's central argument restated from a different angle, and it's worth examining whether that actually holds up.

Looking at the specific mechanisms: the bracket never overreaches past the last measurement, the expectation counts only what the structure permits, the refusal to make novelty claims keeps attribution verifiable, the refusal map locates mechanisms by declining to bracket where monotonicity breaks, the tripwire stays inside the index, the circuit avoids negation and thus paradox — the limitation itself becomes the safety. Even the empty index achieves closure through its own constraint. Every instance of power comes from a refusal, which is a genuinely unifying observation. And it connects back to the no-negation principle: the book is safe because it can't say certain things, the same structural shape throughout.

Now I'm testing whether this holds by weight — can I enumerate which results exist *because* of a refusal rather than assertion? The negative results, the puncture, the dichotomy that can't close exactly, the excluded forms, the three-body maximal case, geometry resisting indexing, the unclosable classification, the bracket's silence outward, E=0 being insufficient. I should count the major results and classify them to see if the claim actually holds.

And the sharpest case: **the empty index is closed, complete, and carries nothing.** Closure alone certifies vacuity as readily as substance. What distinguishes Λ isn't that it closed — it's that it closed while carrying seventeen generators and seven bits it didn't need.

**`zeno.py` implements it.** Work is divided until each piece fits a declared budget, each piece writes its result before the next begins, and a rerun costs only the remainder.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""zeno.py — bounded, checkpointed, resumable execution.

The prime directive: no operation runs unbounded. Every step declares a budget,
writes its result before the next begins, and is skipped on a rerun if it has
already succeeded. Work that exceeds its budget is halved and retried, so a step
that cannot finish whole finishes in pieces rather than not at all.

Three guarantees:
  (i)   nothing is lost to a timeout — the last completed step is on disk
  (ii)  a rerun costs only what has not yet succeeded
  (iii) a step that overruns reports its overrun rather than dying silently

Usage
    from zeno import step, halve, State
    with State("audits") as st:
        n = step(st, "lattice pairs", lambda: count_pairs(L), budget=120)
        for part in halve(cells, budget=90):   # splits until each part fits
            ...
"""
import json, os, time, math, hashlib, sys

ROOT = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), ".zeno")


class State:
    """A named, on-disk record of which steps have completed and what they returned."""

    def __init__(self, name, reset=False):
        self.name = name
        self.path = os.path.join(ROOT, f"{name}.json")
        os.makedirs(ROOT, exist_ok=True)
        if reset and os.path.exists(self.path):
            os.remove(self.path)
        self.done = {}
        if os.path.exists(self.path):
            try:
                self.done = json.load(open(self.path))
            except Exception:
                self.done = {}
        self.t0 = time.time()

    def __enter__(self):
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *a):
        self.flush()
        return False

    def flush(self):
        tmp = self.path + ".tmp"
        json.dump(self.done, open(tmp, "w"))
        os.replace(tmp, self.path)          # atomic: never a half-written state

    def elapsed(self):
        return time.time() - self.t0


def _key(name, salt=""):
    return hashlib.sha256((name + "|" + salt).encode()).hexdigest()[:16]


def step(st, name, fn, budget=120, salt="", force=False):
    """Run fn() once. Skip it on a rerun if it has already succeeded.

    budget is a soft bound in seconds: exceeding it is recorded and reported,
    never suppressed, so a step that is quietly growing is visible before it
    becomes a timeout.
    """
    k = _key(name, salt)
    if not force and k in st.done and st.done[k].get("ok"):
        rec = st.done[k]
        print(f"  · {name}: skipped, done in {rec['secs']:.1f}s")
        return rec["value"]
    t = time.time()
    try:
        v = fn()
        ok, err = True, None
    except Exception as e:                   # a failed step is recorded, not lost
        v, ok, err = None, False, f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"
    secs = time.time() - t
    st.done[k] = {"name": name, "ok": ok, "secs": secs, "value": v, "error": err}
    st.flush()
    mark = "ok " if ok else "FAIL"
    over = "  ** OVER BUDGET **" if secs > budget else ""
    print(f"  {mark} {name}: {secs:.1f}s{over}")
    if err:
        print(f"       {err}")
    return v


def halve(seq, budget=90, probe=64, work=None):
    """Yield slices of seq sized so each is expected to finish inside budget.

    Times a small probe, extrapolates, and halves until the projection fits.
    This is the Zeno part: the interval is divided until it is small enough to
    complete, rather than attempted whole and lost.
    """
    seq = list(seq)
    n = len(seq)
    if n == 0:
        return
    if work is None:
        size = n
    else:
        p = min(probe, n)
        t = time.time()
        work(seq[:p])
        per = max((time.time() - t) / p, 1e-9)
        size = max(1, int(budget / per))
        while size > 1 and size * per > budget:
            size //= 2
    for i in range(0, n, size):
        yield seq[i:i + size]


def report(st):
    d = list(st.done.values())
    ok = sum(1 for r in d if r["ok"])
    slow = [r for r in d if r["ok"] and r["secs"] > 30]
    print(f"\n  zeno: {ok}/{len(d)} steps complete, {st.elapsed():.1f}s this run")
    if slow:
        print("  slowest steps — the ones that will time out first as the book grows:")
        for r in sorted(slow, key=lambda r: -r["secs"])[:5]:
            print(f"    {r['secs']:6.1f}s  {r['name']}")
    bad = [r for r in d if not r["ok"]]
    if bad:
        print("  failed steps, retained for retry:")
        for r in bad:
            print(f"    {r['name']}: {r['error']}")
    return len(bad)

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"## Five findings
**1 · The clock was an assumption, not a law.** The occupancy result was first proved as a theorem about any index whose cells are transitions. It is a theorem about indices whose destinations are **non-accretive**, and empty destinations — which is what §7.1 silently assumes — are sufficient and not necessary. §7.1's two bounds on g read it as *placed* and as *present*, and the two agree only when the destination begins empty. Build the index that distinguishes them and, at the caps of §7.4, **31.6% of composable steps run backwards**. §11.
**2 · Time here is a selection, not a structure.** An index does not have *a* clock. It has **one per coordinate and no others** — sums, max and min all fail to close — each carrying a forward arrow, a backward co-arrow and a timeless core, the two clocks covering the object and meeting in the core. The sixteen combinations are distinct, closed under intersection, never under union, and imposing all of them leaves exactly one component per object. §36–§38.
**3 · The object is a certificate, which closes the antecedent rather than deferring it.** An arrow is a **ranking function** and the maximal sub-index a **supporting invariant**: something an analyst supplies from a class the analyst chooses. **A certificate has nothing to predict.** Asking what the composition order forecasts that something else does not is asking what a proof technique forecasts — so the measurement this paper's title implies is not a hard problem awaiting an apparatus but the wrong request. §40.
**4 · Treeness is the load-bearing hypothesis, and it was never named as one.** The decay theorem, the Markov property, the balance identity and the cut law are four results resting on a single condition: the constraint graph is a tree. **All four fail at Λ₉′**, the one stage of the tower that closes a cycle. §12.11.1's *the tree or the tightness* is not a choice between two presentations; it is the point at which a family of theorems stops applying, and the 93 cells are paid for in theorems. §41.1.
**5 · The framework measures distance from membership where its neighbours settle membership.** Four times in this paper the surrounding literature turned out to have the class and not the count — 2-decomposability, interval-dismantling, the starshaped class, and ranking functions.  propagation of Chapter 15 all use it; §7.1 records treeness as a fact about Λ and never as a
 condition. **A hypothesis that is never stated cannot be checked, and the counterexample has been
 inside this book since the ninth axis.**

 **Λ₉′ is the test, and it separates the results.** Adding 2S′ ≤ 2f+1 closes the cycle f — g — 2S′ — f
 and buys 93 cells of tightness. Measured on both:

  property                                        Λ₉, a tree     Λ₉′, a cycle
  closure, E(X) = 0                               0              **0**
  factorisation over the transfer, defect         0              **0**
  conditional independence, f ⊥ 2S′ given g       0 of 16         **6 of 16**

 fails is conditional independence, and it fails at exactly one cut.

 either graph and the two ends fall apart — in Λ₉′ as much as in Λ₉ — because the cycle lies wholly on
 the target side and does not cross that cut. Remove g and in the tree f and 2S′ fall apart, while in
 Λ₉′ they stay joined by the new edge.

    **A result conditioned on a coordinate holds exactly when that coordinate separates the things
    being conditioned. Treeness is not the hypothesis; it is the condition under which the
    hypothesis holds at every cut at once.**

 In a tree every internal vertex is an articulation point, so the condition is free and nobody notices
 it is being used. Add one edge and it becomes a fact about *which* cut, which is why §12.11.5's
 factorisation survives Λ₉′ and §12.11.1's tightness costs what it costs. **The 93 cells are not paid
 for in generality across the board** — they are paid for at the cuts the new edge spans, and nowhere
 else. Register 347.

 counterexample: Λ₉′ closes a cycle, and **closure survives it (E = 0) and so does the factorisation

Both built in, and defining the hypothesis produced a correction to the paper.

**Time is now §6.2's ninth subject.** What makes it a subject rather than a metaphor is that no coordinate was added to admit it — the other eight are things indexed, and time is *not* indexed. §F.4.3 forbids a date; what enters instead is composition, an order between cells. It is measured: **zero of 739 steps raise occupancy**, three eras pure in occupancy with total circulation inside and none between, 904 of 1,654 cells conservative. **The clock is a coordinate the book already carried, read as an order** — which is why nothing had to be extended to reach it. And it states the method's limit more sharply than any other subject: definability is not reachability, and an index can say completely what a thing *is* while saying almost nothing about what it can *become*.

**On the hypothesis — the paper's finding stands and its statement was one step too broad.** I tested it against the book's own counterexample:

| property | Λ₉, a tree | Λ₉′, a cycle |
|---|---|---|
| closure, E(X) = 0 | 0 | **0** |
| factorisation over q, defect | 0 | **0** |
| conditional independence, f ⊥ 2S′ given g | 0 of 16 | **6 of 16** |

**Closure does not need the tree. Neither does the factorisation.** Both survive the cycle intact. The failure is local, and the reason is exact: remove q and the two ends separate in *both* graphs, because the cycle lies wholly on the target side and never crosses that cut. Remove g and f and 2S′ separate only in the tree.

> **A result conditioned on a coordinate holds exactly when that coordinate separates the things being conditioned. Treeness is not the hypothesis; it is the condition under which the hypothesis holds at every cut at once.**

In a tree every internal vertex is an articulation point, so the condition is free and nobody notices it's being used. That's why it went unnamed for the whole book. And it re-prices Λ₉′: **the 93 cells are not paid for in generality across the board** — only at the cuts the new edge spans.

§12.11.0.01 and §6.2. Entries 347 and 348. **212 pages, 98,110 words**, register 165–348, all twenty audits pass.

from zeno import State, step, report
from method_tower import base
from itertools import combinations
from collections import defaultdict
L=base((3,3,1,3,1)); S=set(L)
J=lambda a,b: tuple(max(x,y) for x,y in zip(a,b))
M=lambda a,b: tuple(min(x,y) for x,y in zip(a,b))
with State("ttp-pushback", reset=True) as st:
    def push():
        j=defaultdict(int); m=defaultdict(int)
        for a,b in combinations(L,2):
            x=J(a,b)
            if x!=a and x!=b: j[x]+=1
            y=M(a,b)
            if y!=a and y!=b: m[y]+=1
        return {c:j[c]+m[c] for c in L}
    P=step(st,"pushback J(x)+M(x) over 475,800 pairs",push,budget=120)
    v=sorted(P.values())
    import statistics
    print(f"     minimum   {min(v)}      (paper 16)")
    print(f"     median    {statistics.median(v):.0f}     (paper 506)")
    print(f"     maximum   {max(v):,}   (paper 5,091)")
    print(f"     mean      {sum(v)/len(v):.0f}     (paper 739)")
    print(f"     removable with no failing pair  {sum(1 for x in v if x==0)}   (paper 0)")
    # J(x)=0 exactly on join-irreducibles

  mean                                          739

 implied back sixteen ways.

 **The floor is not a measurement.** A cell with pushback zero would have to be join-prime *and*
 meet-prime — irreducible on both sides. Λ₈ has eighteen of each and **their intersection is empty**,
 at every cap tested. So zero is unreachable by construction, not by luck.

 **And the minimum that *can* leave follows from the same fact.**

    **X ∖ [a, b] is a sublattice if and only if a is join-prime and b is meet-prime.**

 *Proof.* Let R = [a,b] and suppose z ∈ R with z = x ∨ y and x, y ∉ R. Since x, y ≤ z ≤ b, being
 outside R means x ≱ a and y ≱ a, while a ≤ x ∨ y. In a distributive lattice every join-irreducible is
 join-prime, so a ≤ x ∨ y forces a ≤ x or a ≤ y — contradiction. Conversely if a is join-reducible,
 a = u ∨ v with u, v < a, both under b and neither above a, so u, v ∉ R while u ∨ v = a ∈ R. Dually for
 meets and b. ∎

 across all 471,906 surviving pairs.**

 whose removal the rest of the index does not contradict, because there is no cell irreducible on both
 sides. Register 349.

**§12.11.0.2 — The clock is an assumption, and the assumption can be removed.** This lands directly on the result I registered two entries earlier, which is why it sits immediately after it.

**§7.1's bound g ≤ q reads g as *placed*; g ≤ 2(2f+1) reads it as *present*.** The two coincide only where the destination begins empty, and Λ carries no coordinate for what was already there. So composition's matching condition identifies placed with present — **an assumption about destinations, not a constraint of counting.** That's a **second** conflation in a construction that claims *seven constraints, four origins and nothing else*; register 301 found the first.

Building the index that distinguishes them: **13,775 cells, closed** — and **826,950 of 2,620,090 composable pairs raise occupancy, 31.6%.**

> A closed index of transitions has a one-way clock exactly when its destinations begin empty. **An arrow is worth the size of the assumption it was computed under.**

**What survives is more than what fell.** The maximal sub-index on which a weight never rises is closed, and there is **one per coordinate and no others** — shell 9,407, subshell 9,845, occupancy 5,165, spin 7,160, every size matching the paper exactly. Sums break both sides, max breaks meets, min breaks joins: §18.4.1's cap table now deciding what may be a *clock*. **An index doesn't have a clock; it has one per coordinate**, and occupancy — the one this book built on — is the strictest of the four.

**One recovery worth noting.** The paper's construction is under-specified: its text never says whether 2S′ is bounded by g or by G. My first build gave 6,000 cells. Only **2S′ ≤ G** gives 13,775 — the count settling what the prose left open, which is physically right since a target's multiplicity answers to what is *present*.

Entry 352. **213 pages, 100,036 words**, register 165–352, all twenty audits pass.

**Remaining:** §13's second bridges, §17–22's n-body index and the Brylawski identification, §38–39's meet-semilattice and tree-distance decay, §41's decay theorem.

from zeno import State, step
from method_tower import base
from itertools import combinations
from collections import defaultdict
L=base((3,3,1,3,1))
IX={'n':0,'l':1,'k':2,'q':3,'e':4,'f':5,'g':6,'2S':7}
B=[('g','n'),('2S','e'),('f','2S'),('f','l'),('g','2S'),('e','n'),('l','g'),('g','l'),('e','k'),
   ('k','e'),('n','e'),('l','f'),('2S','g'),('2S','f'),('e','2S'),('n','g'),('k','g'),('e','l'),
   ('k','f'),('n','f')]
Jn=lambda a,b: tuple(max(x,y) for x,y in zip(a,b))
Mt=lambda a,b: tuple(min(x,y) for x,y in zip(a,b))
def price(X):
    S=set(X); j=m=0
    for a,b in combinations(X,2):
        if Jn(a,b) not in S: j+=1
        if Mt(a,b) not in S: m+=1
    A=defaultdict(set); Bq=defaultdict(set)
    for c in X: A[c[3]].add((c[0],c[1],c[2],c[7])); Bq[c[3]].add((c[4],c[5],c[6]))
    return j,m,sum(len(A[q])*len(Bq[q]) for q in A)-len(X)
with State("ttp-bridges", reset=True) as st:
    j0,m0,d0=price(L)
    print(f"  {'bridge':10s} {'cells':>6s} {'join':>5s} {'meet':>5s} {'defect':>7s}")
    print(f"  {'none':10s} {len(L):6,d} {j0:5d} {m0:5d} {d0:7d}")
    rows=[]
    for a,b in B:
        X=[c for c in L if c[IX[a]]<=c[IX[b]]]
        j,m,d=step(st,f"bridge {a} ≤ {b}",lambda X=X: price(X),budget=20)
        rows.append((len(X),j,m,d,f"{a} ≤ {b}"))
    for n,j,m,d,nm in rows:
        print(f"  {nm:10s} {n:6,d} {j:5d} {m:5d} {d:7d}")
    cl=sum(1 for n,j,m,d,_ in rows if j==0 and m==0)
    cyl=sum(1 for n,j,m,d,_ in rows if d==0)
    print(f"\n  closure survives: {cl} of {len(rows)}   (paper: all 20)")
    print(f"  cylinder survives: {cyl} of {len(rows)}   (paper: 5)")
    z=sorted(n for n,j,m,d,_ in rows if d==0)
    print(f"  the defect-zero sets are the smallest: {z}   (paper 48 to 141)")
    nz=[d for n,j,m,d,_ in rows if d>0]
    print(f"  defects among the rest: {min(nz)} to {max(nz)}   (paper 23 to 354)")

from itertools import combinations
from collections import defaultdict
L=base((3,3,1,3,1))
IX={'n':0,'l':1,'k':2,'q':3,'e':4,'f':5,'g':6,'2S':7}
B=[('g','n'),('2S','e'),('f','2S'),('f','l'),('g','2S'),('e','n'),('l','g'),('g','l'),('e','k'),
   ('k','e'),('n','e'),('l','f'),('2S','g'),('2S','f'),('e','2S'),('n','g'),('k','g'),('e','l'),
   ('k','f'),('n','f')]
Jn=lambda a,b: tuple(max(x,y) for x,y in zip(a,b))
Mt=lambda a,b: tuple(min(x,y) for x,y in zip(a,b))
def price(X):
    S=set(X); j=m=0
    for a,b in combinations(X,2):
        if Jn(a,b) not in S: j+=1
        if Mt(a,b) not in S: m+=1
    A=defaultdict(set); Bq=defaultdict(set)
    for c in X: A[c[3]].add((c[0],c[1],c[2],c[7])); Bq[c[3]].add((c[4],c[5],c[6]))
    return j,m,sum(len(A[q])*len(Bq[q]) for q in A)-len(X)
with State("ttp-bridges", reset=True) as st:
    j0,m0,d0=price(L)
    print(f"  {'bridge':10s} {'cells':>6s} {'join':>5s} {'meet':>5s} {'defect':>7s}")
    print(f"  {'none':10s} {len(L):6,d} {j0:5d} {m0:5d} {d0:7d}")
    rows=[]
    for a,b in B:
        X=[c for c in L if c[IX[a]]<=c[IX[b]]]
        j,m,d=step(st,f"bridge {a} ≤ {b}",lambda X=X: price(X),budget=20)
        rows.append((len(X),j,m,d,f"{a} ≤ {b}"))
    for n,j,m,d,nm in rows:
        print(f"  {nm:10s} {n:6,d} {j:5d} {m:5d} {d:7d}")
    cl=sum(1 for n,j,m,d,_ in rows if j==0 and m==0)
    cyl=sum(1 for n,j,m,d,_ in rows if d==0)
    print(f"\n  closure survives: {cl} of {len(rows)}   (paper: all 20)")
    print(f"  cylinder survives: {cyl} of {len(rows)}   (paper: 5)")
    z=sorted(n for n,j,m,d,_ in rows if d==0)
    print(f"  the defect-zero sets are the smallest: {z}   (paper 48 to 141)")
    nz=[d for n,j,m,d,_ in rows if d>0]
    print(f"  defects among the rest: {min(nz)} to {max(nz)}   (paper 23 to 354)")

**§12.11.0.3 — Every second bridge, priced.** All twenty rows of the paper's table reproduce exactly: cells, join and meet failures, and factorisation defects.

**Closure survives all twenty. Sixteen destroy the factorisation**, defects 23 to 354. That separates two properties the book had been treating together:

> **The exclusivity is exclusivity of the tree, not of closure.** E = 0 is untouched by a second bridge; the cylinder is destroyed by it.

And **q is computed to be the unique cut vertex** separating source from target — something §13.2 and §12.6.1 both state as readings and neither states structurally. The mechanism is the spanning-tree identity |E| = |V| − 1: eight nodes, seven edges, so a second bridge costs an existing one or costs a coordinate.

**One correction back to the paper.** Its prose says five bridges leave the factorisation intact and fifteen destroy it. **Its own table — which I match row for row — shows four and sixteen.** The five smallest sets are 48, 60, 120, 141 and 141, and one of the two at 141 carries defect 70. The table is right and the sentence beside it is not. That's the second such disagreement found in this paper, both between prose and a table the prose is describing.

**And a failure of my own worth more than the result.** I renumbered by patching four times, collided twice, and ended with two sections sharing a label — caught by SEQUENCE both times. The cause was arithmetic on labels: each insertion shifted its neighbours by hand, **and a hand shift is a literal**. Repaired by the move that should have been first — read the sections in physical order, assign numbers sequentially, remap every reference **by the title it points at rather than by the number**. One pass, no collisions.

**A label is a name, not an address.** Entry 354 states it beside register 351's converse: an instrument must not name a thing by a label the book can change, and an author must not compute a label by hand.

**215 pages, 100,790 words**, register 165–354, all twenty pass.

**Remaining:** §17–22's n-body index and the Brylawski identification, §38–39's meet-semilattice and tree-distance decay, §41's decay theorem.

from zeno import State, step
from itertools import combinations
def exact(n,N):
    out=[]
    def rec(pref,prev,tot):
        k=len(pref)
        if k==n: out.append(tuple(pref)); return
        for m in range(0,prev+1):
            if tot+m>N: break
            rec(pref+[tot+m],m,tot+m)
    rec([],N,0)
    return out
def envelope(n,N):
    out=[]
    def rec(pref):
        k=len(pref)
        if k==n: out.append(tuple(pref)); return
        lo=pref[-1] if pref else 0
        hi=N if not pref else min(N,(pref[-1]*(k+1))//k)
        for v in range(lo,hi+1): rec(pref+[v])
    rec([])
    return out
Jn=lambda a,b: tuple(max(x,y) for x,y in zip(a,b))
Mt=lambda a,b: tuple(min(x,y) for x,y in zip(a,b))
def fails(X):
    S=set(X); j=m=0
    for a,b in combinations(X,2):
        if Jn(a,b) not in S: j+=1
        if Mt(a,b) not in S: m+=1
    return j,m
with State("ttp-nbody", reset=True) as st:

new = """### 12.11.0.6 Past, present and future — a path, not a triangle
 §10.2 reads the constraint tree as past — change — future. **That reading has arithmetic, and it is
 not the arithmetic of three free things.**

 **Treated as independent the three parts overcount by 130%**: |A|·|Q|·|B| = 33 · 4 · 17 = 2,244
 against |Λ| = 976, a defect of 1,268. Conditioned on the transfer they separate exactly, defect zero.

 **And the balance is not special to the transfer.** Every two-sided cut of the tree gives it —
 **ℓ, q, f and g, all defect zero.** §12.6.1 presents the factorisation as though the transfer were
 doing the work; the computation says the *tree* is doing it, and q is distinguished only by which two
 things it separates.

 **The shape is a path.** Two edges, past ↔ present and present ↔ future, and no past–future edge —
 treewidth 1. By §18.4.1 treewidth 1 closes exactly and treewidth 2 gives an envelope, so **Λ's
 exactness is a proof that the three parts are not a triangle.** A triangle would be the three-body
 shape and register 316 states its price.

 **The future is never a value.** Of **97** (past, present) pairs, **none determines a single future** —
 futures per pair run 5, median 10, maximum 17. And for each value of the present, **every past gives
 the same future set**:

  present q     distinct pasts    distinct future sets    |future|
  0                        33                       1            5
  1                        33                       1           10
  2                        23                       1           15
  3                         8                       1           17

    **The future is conditionally independent of the past given the present** — a Markov property,
    exact at every value. The past constrains only which presents are reachable; having spent that,
    it has spent everything.

 The dependence is monotone and opposed: the future set nests increasing, 5 ⊂ 10 ⊂ 15 ⊂ 17, while the
 past set nests decreasing, 33 ⊇ 33 ⊇ 23 ⊇ 8. **And the bracket is saturated** — at every present the
 admissible future is the full interval between its own extremes, nothing inside missing. E(X) = 0 read
 on the target end.

 **The tick, decomposed.** Over the 1,169 composable cells the clock ticks 0, 1 or 2 — 389, 540, 240 —
 and the tick has two sources: k − g = (k − q) + (q − g), *something not removed* and *something
 removed but not placed*. **430 against 430**, and the split table is its own transpose: (0,1) = 270
 against (1,0) = 270, (0,2) = 80 against (2,0) = 80.

    **Irreversibility has two independent sources contributing identically.** One is a choice not
    taken; the other a capacity that could not receive. The index weights them the same.

 **And Pauli is a minority partner in it.** g's ceiling is fixed by counting in 60.2% of composable
 cells, tied in 29.5%, and by shell capacity in only 10.3%. **The arrow of time in this object is
 overwhelmingly a counting phenomenon**, which §12.9 states in advance. Register 357.

""" + anchor
assert s.count(anchor)==1
s=s.replace(anchor,new)
i=s.index('### 26.7.7'); j=s.index('### 26.8')
blk=s[i:j].rstrip('\n')
e=""" 357. Past, present and future given their arithmetic at §12.11.0.6, every figure reproducing. Treated
 as free the three parts overcount by 130% — 2,244 against 976 — and conditioned on the transfer they
 separate exactly. **The balance holds at every two-sided cut of the tree, not only at q**: ℓ, f and g
 give defect zero too, so §12.6.1 attributes to the transfer what the tree is doing. **The future is
 never a value** — none of 97 (past, present) pairs determines one — and **for each present every past
 gives the same future set**, a Markov property exact at all four values. The shape is a path and not a
 triangle, which is why Λ closes exactly. **And the tick has two sources contributing identically** —
 430 cells where something was not removed against 430 where something was removed and not placed, the
 split table its own transpose. Pauli fixes g's ceiling in only 10.3% of composable cells: the arrow
 here is a counting phenomenon, not a coupling one.

"""
s=s[:i]+blk+'\n\n'+e+s[j:]
s=re.sub(r'([Tt])hree hundred and fifty-six(?! corrections)', lambda m:m.group(1)+'hree hundred and fifty-seven', s)
s=s.replace('three hundred and fifty-six corrections','three hundred and fifty-seven corrections')
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
# renumber from physical order, per register 354
hd=[(m.group(1),m.group(2)) for m in re.finditer(r'^### (12\.11\.0\.\d+) (.+)$',s,re.M)]
newmap={ti:f"12.11.0.{n}" for n,(lab,ti) in enumerate(hd,1)}
oldref={lab:ti for lab,ti in hd}
s=re.sub(r'^### 12\.11\.0\.\d+ (.+)$', lambda m: f"### {newmap[m.group(1)]} {m.group(1)}", s, flags=re.M)
tok={lab:f"\x02{i:02d}\x03" for i,lab in enumerate(oldref)}
for lab in sorted(oldref,key=len,reverse=True): s=re.sub(r'§'+re.escape(lab)+r'\b','§'+tok[lab],s)
for lab,t in tok.items(): s=s.replace(t,newmap[oldref[lab]])
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
seq=[m.group(1) for m in re.finditer(r'^### (12\.11\.0\.\d+)',s,re.M)]
key=lambda t:[int(v) for v in t.split('.')[1:]]
print("sections:",seq,"| monotone",seq==sorted(seq,key=key))
print("unresolved:",sorted(set(re.findall(r'§(12\.11\.0\.\d+)',s))-set(seq)) or "none")

The remaining **119 are results**, averaging about 140 words against §26.7.4's standard of 29. cd /home/claude/book && cp "The Method 1.3.md" C1.bak && python3 << 'PYEOF'
import re, hashlib
p='The Method 1.3.md'; s=open(p,encoding='utf-8').read()
W=lambda t: len(re.sub(r'[*#`|]','',t).split())
NEW={
204:" 204. Four figure captions written before the figures were read; two misdescribed what they showed. Recaptioned from the rendered images.",
205:" 205. §23.6.3 called a bracketed value a prediction. Withdrawn by the author: it is a deduction from measured neighbours under monotonicity, not a forecast.",
208:" 208. The tower session recomputed the self-duality count under the wrong reflection — max + min − x against the book's max − x — and recorded 8 as unreproduced. Both counts are right about their own map.",
211:" 211. Appendix D's closure was asserted rather than enumerated, a distinction the book had already ruled against itself at E.4.1 and not applied here. Enumerated.",
212:" 212. Two cells the mathematical fibre of Q admits and Q lacks, exposed by items L and M. E(Q) = 2 fibred, 1 unfibred.",
214:" 214. Two obligations stated in the prose and absent from the index of open questions — a seniority literature and a coverage recomputation — recovered as admitted-and-absent cells of Q.",
216:" 216. The contents was maintained beside the book rather than derived from it, which is what let 215 happen. It is now generated from the headings at build time and cannot disagree.",
217:" 217. Four places called a bracketed value *the prediction* after it had been withdrawn. The withdrawal repaired one and left the class.",
222:" 222. Item L closed. Five results the table had no room for are all theorem · order, placed by reading each proof rather than its subject; A.5's verification was sampled and is now exhaustive.",
223:" 223. Two literature searches run and recorded at §27.10, neither returning a precedent and neither establishing anything — a search performed is a search that goes in the record.",
224:" 224. **The book's central theorem has a precedent.** A.2 — X closed ⟺ ℛ(X) = X — is Bergman's Double-projection Theorem specialised to products of chains, itself a consequence of Baker–Pixley 1975. Correct, and fifty years late.",
225:" 225. §27.12 lists five results with no located source, each with a definition, the search run, a confirming test and a falsifier. Not a novelty claim, which §27.1 forbids.",
}
i=s.index('### 26.7.7'); j=s.index('### 26.7.8')
sec=s[i:j]
st=[m.start() for m in re.finditer(r'^\s{0,3}\d{3}\.\s',sec,re.M)]
head=sec[:st[0]]
ents=[sec[st[q]:(st[q+1] if q+1<len(st) else len(sec))] for q in range(len(st))]
before=0; out=[]
for t in ents:
    n=int(re.match(r'\s{0,3}(\d{3})',t).group(1))
    if n in NEW:
        before+=W(t); out.append(NEW[n]+"\n\n")
    else: out.append(t)
s=s[:i]+head+''.join(out)+s[j:]
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(s)
after=sum(W(NEW[n]) for n in NEW)
print(f"batch 1: {len(NEW)} entries, {before:,} words -> {after:,}   saving {before-after:,}")
reg=s[s.rindex('## 26. Withdrawals'):s.rindex('## 27.')]
nums=set()
for mm in re.finditer(r'^\s{0,3}((?:\d{3}, )*\d{3})\.\s',reg,re.M):
    nums|={int(x) for x in re.findall(r'\d{3}',mm.group(1))}
print("numbers absent everywhere:",[x for x in range(199,363) if x not in nums] or "none")
print(f"register {W(reg):,} words")
PYEOF
python3 "The Method 1.3 press.py" 2>&1|tail -1
timeout 1800 python3 "The Method 1.3 audits.py" | tail -3

import re, importlib.util
from collections import defaultdict
from itertools import product
